lessons.title: V3·F1 — CTEs, materialization and readable query architecture
lessons.summary: Lesson 14 taught you what WITH does. This one is about what it costs and what it buys: the PostgreSQL 12 inlining rule, AS MATERIALIZED as a deliberate fence, data-modifying CTEs and the snapshot they share, and the grain discipline that makes a hundred-line report reviewable.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·F1 — CTEs, materialization and readable query architecture

Lesson 14 sold you the readability argument for `WITH`, and it was true:
naming an intermediate result turns a nest of parentheses into a pipeline
you can read top to bottom. What lesson 14 did not tell you is that a CTE
is also a **planner boundary you can turn on and off**, that referencing
one twice changes how PostgreSQL executes it, and that a `WITH` clause can
contain an `UPDATE`. Those three facts are the difference between someone
who writes CTEs because their team's style guide says to, and someone who
uses them as an architectural tool.

## Concept

The first thing to internalise is the rule PostgreSQL 12 introduced.

```sql
WITH recent AS (
    SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid'
)
SELECT count(*) FROM recent WHERE total > 500;
```

Before 12, `recent` was an **optimisation fence**: PostgreSQL evaluated it
completely, into a tuplestore, and only then applied `total > 500`. That
meant scanning and storing 250,472 rows to count a fraction of them.
Since 12, a CTE that is **not recursive**, **has no side effects**, and is
**referenced exactly once** is inlined — folded into the outer query like
any subquery — so `total > 500` is pushed down into the scan and nothing is
materialised at all.

All three conditions matter. Break any one and you get the old behaviour:

```sql
WITH cat AS (                                   -- referenced twice below,
    SELECT category, sum(price) AS revenue      -- so NOT inlined
    FROM products GROUP BY category
)
SELECT category, revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / (SELECT sum(revenue) FROM cat), 2) AS pct
FROM cat;
```

That is usually what you want — the expensive aggregate runs once and both
references read the same stored result. But it is a decision the planner
made for you based on a reference count, which is a proxy for intent, not
intent itself. So PostgreSQL lets you say it out loud:

```sql
WITH heavy AS MATERIALIZED     ( ... )   -- always evaluate once, into a store
WITH light AS NOT MATERIALIZED ( ... )   -- always inline, even if used twice
```

`AS MATERIALIZED` is the tool when a CTE is expensive and referenced more
than once, or when inlining would let the planner push a predicate somewhere
that makes it slower (a common case: the CTE contains a `LIMIT`-shaped or
sorted intermediate you want computed exactly once). `AS NOT MATERIALIZED`
is the tool when you referenced a cheap CTE twice for readability and do not
want a tuplestore for it.

**The second fact: `WITH` can modify data.**

```sql
WITH touched AS (
    UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped'
    WHERE status = 'paid' AND id <= 1000
    RETURNING id, customer_id, total
)
SELECT count(*) AS moved, sum(total) AS value FROM touched;
```

Every sub-statement in a data-modifying CTE runs against **the same
snapshot**. The `SELECT` above cannot see the `UPDATE`'s effect through the
`orders` table — only through the `RETURNING` rows the CTE hands it. Two
data-modifying CTEs touching the same row do not see each other either, and
their execution order is undefined. This is not a wart; it is what makes the
statement atomic and predictable. It is also the single most misunderstood
corner of the feature.

**The third fact: architecture is grain discipline.** The reason a report
CTE pipeline is readable is not the indentation. It is that each named step
answers "one row per what?" and the name says so. `revenue_per_category` is
a contract. `t2` is not.

## Exercise 1 — name one step

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Revenue by customer country over paid orders only.
Put the paid-orders filter in a named CTE, then join `customers` in the
outer query. Columns, in order: `country`, `orders`, `revenue`
(`sum(total)`). Any row order. Twelve countries exist; you will get at most
that many rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex1`

## Exercise 2 — a three-step pipeline

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Line-item revenue rolled up to category, in three
named steps: line revenue → per product → per category. Columns:
`category`, `products` (how many distinct products in that category sold
anything), `revenue` (`sum(quantity * price)`). Exclude cancelled orders.
**Ordered by `revenue` descending.** Six rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex2`

## Exercise 3 — aggregate each side, then join

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Per country: how many customers, how many orders
they placed, and their total revenue — with countries whose customers have
never ordered still showing, as zeros. Columns: `country`, `customers`,
`orders`, `revenue`. Any order. Aggregate each side separately and join the
small results.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex3`

## Exercise 4 — reference the CTE twice

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Category revenue with each category's share of the
whole. Columns: `category`, `revenue`, `pct` (revenue as a percentage of
total revenue, rounded to 2 decimals). Use `order_items` joined to
`products`, all orders. **Ordered by `revenue` descending.**

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex4`

## Exercise 5 — the two-stage aggregate

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The distribution of order counts: for each number
of orders, how many customers placed exactly that many. Columns:
`orders_per_customer`, `customers`. **Ordered by `orders_per_customer`
ascending.** Write the per-customer count as `AS MATERIALIZED` and be able
to say why the keyword changes nothing about the answer.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex5`

## Exercise 6 — the filter that must come after

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. The top three products by revenue in each category,
with each one's share of its category's revenue. Columns: `category`,
`product_id`, `revenue`, `pct_of_category`, `rn` (1, 2, 3). **Ordered by
`category` ascending, then `rn` ascending.**

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex6`

## Exercise 7 — a data-modifying CTE

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Touch every pending order with `id <= 5000` —
`SET status = status`, deliberately a no-op — and report what you touched
from the `RETURNING` rows, not from the table. Columns: `rows_touched`,
`value` (`sum(total)` rounded to 2 decimals). One row.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex7`

## Exercise 8 — the long report

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. A country scorecard from five named steps.
Columns: `country`, `customers`, `buyers` (customers with at least one
non-cancelled order), `revenue`, `aov` (revenue / orders, 2 decimals),
`items_per_order` (line items per non-cancelled order, 2 decimals).
Non-cancelled orders throughout. **Ordered by `revenue` descending.**

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex8`

## Challenge — the best category per country

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. For each country, the single category its
customers spend most on, with that spend and its share of the country's
total. Columns: `country`, `category`, `category_revenue`,
`country_revenue`, `pct`. Ties broken by `category` ascending. **Ordered by
`country` ascending.** Non-cancelled orders only.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: per category, the number of **distinct orders** that contained
at least one product from it, and the line revenue. Columns: `category`,
`orders`, `revenue`. Any order. The trap is in the first number.

# Reading - v3f01_cte_architecture

A CTE is three unrelated features wearing one keyword: a name for a
subquery, an optional planner fence, and a place to put a data-modifying
statement. Lesson 14 taught the first. This sector is about the other two,
and about the discipline that makes the first one worth anything.

## Notes

**Inlining has exactly three conditions.** Not recursive, no side effects,
referenced once. Miss any and PostgreSQL materialises the CTE into a
tuplestore. The consequence people trip over is the *reference count*:
adding a second, innocuous reference to a CTE — a sanity-check column, a
`WHERE EXISTS` — silently flips a query from "predicate pushed into the
scan" to "scan everything, store it, then filter". The query did not get
slower because of the thing you added; it got slower because of what your
addition told the planner.

**`EXPLAIN` tells you which happened.** An inlined CTE leaves no trace: you
see the scan and the filter fused. A materialised one appears as a `CTE
Scan` node above a `CTE <name>` subplan. If you cannot find a `CTE Scan`,
your CTE was inlined. That is the whole diagnostic.

**`AS MATERIALIZED` is a statement of intent, not a performance trick.**
Reach for it when (a) the CTE is expensive and referenced more than once, or
(b) inlining lets the planner push a qualifier into a place where it changes
the cost badly — classically, into a subquery over a huge table where the
predicate is unindexed, so pushdown converts one aggregate pass into many.
Reach for `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` when a cheap CTE is referenced twice and you
would rather the planner see through it. Both are Part 5 instruments: read
the plan first, then decide.

**Materialising costs memory then disk.** A tuplestore lives in `work_mem`
and spills to a temporary file beyond it. Materialising a CTE that produces
a million wide rows is a real I/O decision, not a free fence. This is why
"just add MATERIALIZED" is bad advice and "materialise the *small* expensive
result, inline the big cheap one" is good advice.

**Data-modifying CTEs share one snapshot.** All sub-statements of a single
statement see the database as of the statement's start. An `UPDATE` inside a
CTE is invisible to a sibling `SELECT` reading the same table; the only way
to see what it did is `RETURNING`. Sibling data-modifying CTEs have no
defined execution order relative to each other, so two of them updating the
same row is a bug you cannot reason about. Use the pattern for
move-and-report (`DELETE ... RETURNING` feeding an `INSERT`), not for
read-your-own-write.

**Aggregate, then join.** The oldest report bug in the world is joining
`customers → orders → order_items` and then counting something. After the
second join each customer appears once per line item, so `count(*)` counts
line items and `sum(total)` counts each order's total once per line on it.
The cure is not `DISTINCT`; the cure is to never create the duplicates —
aggregate each branch to its own grain, then join the small results on the
key. It is also usually faster, because the join happens on twelve rows
instead of a million.

**A CTE cannot see the outer row.** It is a standalone relation, computed
without reference to the query that uses it. "For each row of A, run this
against B" is `LATERAL` (lesson 48) or a correlated subquery. If you find
yourself wanting to pass a column into a CTE, you have chosen the wrong
tool.

**The spectrum.** Subquery → CTE → view → materialized view → temp table is
one axis: how long the intermediate lives and who else can see it. A CTE
lives for one statement and is private. A view is a named query anyone can
use and stores nothing. A materialized view stores rows and goes stale. A
temp table lives for the session and can be indexed. Choose by lifetime and
audience, not by taste.

## ex1 — name one step

What this tested: that filtering is a step worth naming. The classic mistake
is putting `status = 'paid'` in the outer `WHERE` after the join, which
gives the same answer and reads worse — and, in a longer query, hides the
population from the reviewer. `paid_orders` is a sentence; the reviewer can
check it in isolation.

## ex2 — a three-step pipeline

What this tested: keeping the grain visible as it changes. Line → product →
category is three different "one row per what?" answers, and naming each one
is what lets you verify the middle. The classic mistake is collapsing all
three into one `GROUP BY category` with a join — which works here, and stops
working the moment the middle step needs its own filter.

## ex3 — aggregate each side, then join

What this tested: the fan-out cure, plus the honesty of a `LEFT JOIN`. A
country whose customers have never ordered has no rows on the orders side; a
plain join drops it and the report quietly says that country does not exist.
`LEFT JOIN` plus `coalesce` on the measures — never on the key — says zero
instead. The classic mistake is `coalesce(country, 'unknown')`, which papers
over a join you got backwards.

## ex4 — reference the CTE twice

What this tested: the inlining rule made visible. Two references means one
evaluation into a tuplestore, which is precisely what you want here — the
alternative would be computing the category aggregate twice. Notice that
`sum(revenue)` in the scalar subquery sums *six* numbers, not a million; the
CTE changed the grain before the total was taken. The classic mistake is
dividing by `sum(quantity * price)` over the raw table again, which is the
same number computed the expensive way.

## ex5 — the two-stage aggregate

What this tested: an aggregate over the result of an aggregate — the shape
`GROUP BY` alone cannot express. `AS MATERIALIZED` changes nothing about the
answer and that is the point: it is a plan directive, not semantics. The
classic mistake is trying `count(count(*))`, which PostgreSQL rejects
because aggregates do not nest.

## ex6 — the filter that must come after

What this tested: window functions are computed after grouping and before
the outer query's filter, so "top three per category" needs two levels — one
that ranks over the whole category, one that keeps the top rows. Pushing
`rn <= 3` inside would be meaningless (`rn` does not exist yet) and pushing
the *category revenue total* inside after filtering would compute the share
against three products instead of all of them. The classic mistake is
computing `pct_of_category` in the outer query from the surviving rows.

## ex7 — a data-modifying CTE

What this tested: `RETURNING` as the only channel out of a DML CTE. The
update is deliberately a no-op — `SET status = status` — so the exercise is
repeatable, but PostgreSQL still writes a new row version for every row it
touches, which is a real cost and a real vacuum consequence (lesson 44). The
classic mistake is adding a second CTE that reads `orders` to "check" the
update, and being confused that it shows the old state. It shows the
snapshot. There is no old state and no new state inside one statement.

## ex8 — the long report

What this tested: whether five steps stay legible. The interesting column is
`buyers` versus `customers`: two different grains, from two different
populations, joined at the end. The classic mistake is computing `aov` as
`avg(total)` over line-joined rows, which weights each order by how many
items it contained.

## challenge — the best category per country

What this tested: pipeline plus a per-group top-1, plus a share computed
against a total from a different grain. `DISTINCT ON` and
`row_number() = 1` are both correct; the tie-break has to be explicit either
way, or the answer is not reproducible.

## review1 — distinct orders per category

The trap is `count(*)`: an order containing three toys contributes three
`order_items` rows, so `count(*)` counts lines and `count(DISTINCT
o.id)` counts orders. Both are legitimate numbers; only one answers the
question asked. Ask which one the reader will subtract from what.

## Further reading

- [`WITH` Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — the `MATERIALIZED` rules and the snapshot semantics of data-modifying CTEs, stated precisely.
- [`SELECT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — where `WITH` sits in the clause order, and the restrictions on data-modifying sub-statements.
- [Using `EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — how a `CTE Scan` node reads, which is how you tell inlined from materialised.
- [Resource Consumption — `work_mem`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/runtime-config-resource.html) — what a tuplestore costs before and after it spills.
- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the scalar-subquery form ex4 uses against its own CTE.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·F1 — CTEs, materialization and readable query architecture

The archive version. Lesson 14 gave you `WITH`; this is the engineering
treatment — what the planner does with it, what it costs, and how to lay out
a report that a colleague can review without a phone call.

## 1. The inlining rule, exactly

Since PostgreSQL 12, a CTE is **inlined into the outer query** if all three
hold:

1. it is not `RECURSIVE`;
2. it has no side effects (no `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`MERGE` inside);
3. it is referenced **exactly once** in the rest of the query.

Otherwise it is **materialised**: evaluated to completion into a tuplestore,
which the outer query then scans.

```sql
-- inlined: total > 500 is pushed into the scan of orders
WITH paid AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid')
SELECT count(*) FROM paid WHERE total > 500;

-- materialised: two references
WITH paid AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid')
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM paid) AS n,
       (SELECT sum(total) FROM paid) AS v;
```

You can override in either direction:

```sql
WITH paid AS MATERIALIZED     (SELECT ...)   -- fence, always
WITH paid AS NOT MATERIALIZED (SELECT ...)   -- inline, always
```

`NOT MATERIALIZED` is refused for recursive and data-modifying CTEs, because
those cannot be inlined at all.

### Reading the plan

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
WITH paid AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid')
SELECT count(*) FROM paid WHERE total > 500;
```

A materialised CTE shows as:

```
Aggregate
  ->  CTE Scan on paid  (rows=...)
        Filter: (total > 500)
        CTE paid
          ->  Seq Scan on orders
                Filter: (status = 'paid')
```

Two things to notice: the `Filter` sits on the `CTE Scan`, meaning every
paid order was stored and then discarded; and the `CTE paid` subplan is a
separate node with its own row count. Drop `MATERIALIZED` and both nodes
vanish — one `Seq Scan` with both filters fused.

## 2. When materialisation is right

- **Expensive and reused.** An aggregate over a million rows referenced
  three times: materialise, or pay for it three times. (The planner already
  does this for you at two references; saying it is documentation.)
- **Pushdown would hurt.** If inlining lets the planner push a selective-
  looking but unindexed predicate into a subquery that then loses a hash
  aggregate in favour of a nested loop, the fence is cheaper. You discover
  this by reading two plans, not by guessing.
- **You want a stable intermediate for a self-join.** Materialising once and
  joining the store to itself beats computing it twice.

And when it is wrong:

- **The CTE is huge.** A million-row tuplestore that exceeds `work_mem`
  spills to a temp file. You have converted a streaming plan into a write
  and a read.
- **You are using it as a hint instead of an index.** If the real problem is
  that `orders.customer_id` has no index, a fence will not save you.

## 3. Data-modifying CTEs

```sql
WITH archived AS (
    DELETE FROM events WHERE ts < '2023-10-15'
    RETURNING id, customer_id, event_type, payload, ts
)
INSERT INTO events_archive
SELECT * FROM archived;
```

Move-and-report in one atomic statement: the rows are deleted and inserted
together or not at all. The rules that matter:

- **One snapshot.** Every sub-statement sees the database as of statement
  start. A `SELECT` sibling cannot observe the `DELETE`.
- **`RETURNING` is the only output channel.** Without it the CTE yields
  nothing.
- **Sibling order is undefined.** Two DML CTEs touching the same rows are
  unreasoning-about-able. Do not.
- **Triggers still fire**, and they *do* see effects, in trigger-defined
  order. This is where the mental model earns its keep.
- A data-modifying CTE that nothing references still runs. Its execution is
  not conditional on being selected from.

## 4. Grain discipline

Every named step should have an answer to "one row per what?" written into
its name. The fan-out bug:

```sql
-- WRONG: each customer duplicated once per line item
SELECT c.country, count(*) AS customers, sum(o.total) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o      ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY c.country;
```

`customers` counts line items; `revenue` counts each order's total once per
line on that order. The `DISTINCT` patch —
`count(DISTINCT c.id)`, `sum(DISTINCT o.total)` — is worse than wrong: the
second one is *actively incorrect*, because two different orders can share a
total and `DISTINCT` will drop one. The cure:

```sql
WITH cust AS (
    SELECT country, count(*) AS customers FROM customers GROUP BY country
), rev AS (
    SELECT c.country, count(*) AS orders, sum(o.total) AS revenue
    FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.country
)
SELECT cust.country, cust.customers,
       coalesce(rev.orders, 0) AS orders,
       coalesce(rev.revenue, 0) AS revenue
FROM cust LEFT JOIN rev USING (country);
```

Each branch aggregates at its own grain; the join happens on twelve rows.

## 5. Window functions and the two-level pattern

Clause order is `FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window functions →
SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT`. A window function therefore cannot be
filtered in the same query level that computes it:

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT p.category, i.product_id,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category
                              ORDER BY sum(i.quantity * i.price) DESC,
                                       i.product_id) AS rn,
           sum(sum(i.quantity * i.price)) OVER (PARTITION BY p.category)
               AS cat_revenue
    FROM order_items i JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category, i.product_id
)
SELECT category, product_id, revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / cat_revenue, 2) AS pct_of_category, rn
FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category, rn;
```

The nested aggregate `sum(sum(...)) OVER (...)` is legal and often
surprising: the inner `sum` is the group's aggregate, the outer one is a
window over the grouped rows. It is how you get a group total onto every row
of the group without a second pass.

## 6. Common mistakes

- Adding a second reference to a CTE and being surprised the plan changed.
- Using `AS MATERIALIZED` on a huge intermediate and spilling `work_mem`.
- Expecting a sibling `SELECT` to see a DML CTE's writes.
- `sum(DISTINCT x)` as a fan-out patch. It is not one.
- Computing a percentage against the filtered set instead of the population.
- Naming steps `t1`, `t2`, `t3`, then wondering why review found nothing.
- Reaching for a CTE when the requirement is per-outer-row — that is
  `LATERAL`.
- Assuming a CTE is still an optimisation fence because a blog post from
  2016 said so.

## 7. The interview answer

> *"Are CTEs slower than subqueries in PostgreSQL?"*

"Not since 12. A non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced once is
inlined, so it plans identically to the equivalent subquery — you pay
nothing for the readability. It is materialised when it is recursive, when
it modifies data, or when it is referenced more than once, and in that last
case materialising is usually the right call anyway because it means the
work happens once. If I need to override the default I say `AS
MATERIALIZED` or `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` explicitly, and I decide that from
two `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` runs, not from instinct. The `CTE Scan` node is how
you tell which one you got."

## Check yourself

1. State the three conditions for inlining, and name the plan node that
   proves a CTE was materialised instead.
2. You add a harmless second reference to a CTE and the query gets four
   times slower. What changed, and what is the one-word fix if you want the
   old plan back?
3. Why is `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` rejected on a recursive CTE?
4. Where does a materialised CTE's data live, and what happens when it
   exceeds `work_mem`?
5. Inside `WITH x AS (UPDATE t SET ... RETURNING *) SELECT count(*) FROM t`,
   what does the count reflect, and why?
6. Two data-modifying CTEs update the same row. What does PostgreSQL
   guarantee about the outcome?
7. Explain why `sum(DISTINCT o.total)` is a worse fan-out fix than
   aggregating before joining.
8. Write the two-level shape for "top N per group with each row's share of
   its group total", and say why one level cannot do it.
9. What does `sum(sum(x)) OVER (PARTITION BY g)` compute, and at what grain
   is each `sum` evaluated?
10. Give one case where a temp table beats a CTE, and one where a
    materialized view beats both.
11. A colleague wants to pass the outer query's `customer_id` into a CTE.
    What do you tell them to use instead?
12. Your report joins three tables and then counts customers. Name the two
    numbers that are now wrong and the restructuring that fixes both.
