# The long read — what `WITH` actually is

## A feature that arrived twice

Common table expressions entered the SQL standard in SQL:1999, and
PostgreSQL shipped them in 8.4 (2009), recursion included from day one. For
the first decade of their life in PostgreSQL they carried a property that
was never in the standard and never documented as a promise, but which every
serious user relied on: a CTE was an **optimisation fence**. Whatever was
inside it got evaluated, in full, into a tuplestore, before the outer query
saw a row of it.

That property was an implementation artefact that became a feature. People
used it deliberately — to stop the planner pushing a qualifier into a
subquery where a volatile function would then be called a million times; to
force a materialisation the cost model refused to choose; to break a badly
estimated plan into two well estimated halves. Query-tuning folklore from
2010 to 2018 is full of "wrap it in a CTE to fence the planner".

It also silently punished everyone who used CTEs for what they are for. A
junior analyst who wrote a readable five-step pipeline paid, at every step,
for a full materialisation of an intermediate that the planner could have
streamed. The same query written with nested subqueries ran faster and read
worse. That is a bad incentive to put in a language.

PostgreSQL 12 (2019) fixed it, carefully. The commit that did it did not
just remove the fence; it defined precisely when the fence remains, and gave
users explicit syntax for both behaviours. That is the design worth
admiring: the default now matches intent (readability is free), the old
behaviour is still reachable (`AS MATERIALIZED`), and the *new* behaviour is
also forceable (`AS NOT MATERIALIZED`) for cases the reference-count
heuristic gets wrong.

## What the executor does

For an inlined CTE, nothing special happens at all. The rewriter substitutes
the CTE's query into the outer query's range table as a subquery, and from
that point the planner treats it like any other subquery: it may pull the
subquery up into the parent, push qualifiers down through it, reorder joins
across it, and choose scan methods with full knowledge of the outer
predicates. There is no CTE at run time.

For a materialised CTE, the planner produces a `CTE` subplan and the
executor builds a **tuplestore**: an ordered, re-readable buffer that lives
in `work_mem` and spills to a temporary file on disk when it outgrows it.
Each reference in the outer query becomes a `CTE Scan` node that reads the
tuplestore from the start. Because it is re-readable, N references cost one
evaluation and N scans — which is exactly the property that makes
materialisation the right default for a multiply-referenced CTE.

Two consequences follow that surprise people. First, statistics: the planner
estimates the CTE's output rows from the subplan, but it has no column
statistics for the stored result, so predicates applied *above* the `CTE
Scan` are estimated with default selectivities. A materialised CTE is
therefore an estimation cliff; join order decisions above it are made half
blind. Second, memory: a wide intermediate is stored in full, columns you
never use included. `SELECT *` inside a materialised CTE is a real cost, not
a style question.

## Data-modifying CTEs and the snapshot

PostgreSQL 9.1 added `WITH` support for `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE`
(and, in 15, `MERGE` as a target — though `MERGE` may not appear inside a
CTE until later versions; check your release notes). The semantics chosen
were the only ones that could be coherent: all sub-statements of one
top-level statement execute with the **same command snapshot**, so none of
them can see any other's effects through a table.

This makes a statement like

```sql
WITH moved AS (DELETE FROM staging RETURNING *)
INSERT INTO final SELECT * FROM moved;
```

atomic in a way that two statements in a transaction are not: there is no
instant at which the row exists in neither table, and no possibility of the
second statement seeing a row the first did not return. It also makes

```sql
WITH bump AS (UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1)
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;
```

return the **old** balance, forever, no matter how you squint. There is no
ordering you can impose to change that. The answer is not to fight it but to
select from `bump`'s `RETURNING` list instead.

The genuinely dangerous corner is two data-modifying CTEs whose target rows
overlap. Their relative order is unspecified, and because they share a
snapshot, the second one to physically execute may attempt to update a row
version the first already superseded — producing a result that depends on
execution order you cannot control. The documentation says "try to avoid",
which is documentation-speak for "this is undefined behaviour with a polite
face". Triggers add a further wrinkle: they run in trigger order and *do*
observe the effects of earlier sub-statements, so a `BEFORE` trigger can see
a world the sibling `SELECT` cannot.

## Performance notes worth carrying

- **Inlined does not mean free.** Inlining exposes the CTE body to the outer
  predicates, which is usually good and occasionally catastrophic: a
  qualifier pushed into a query containing a volatile or expensive function
  can multiply that function's call count by the row count.
- **Materialised does not mean cached.** The tuplestore lives for the
  statement. Two statements referencing the same CTE text build it twice.
  That is what a temp table or a materialized view is for.
- **`work_mem` is per node, not per query.** A plan with three materialised
  CTEs and two sorts can allocate five times `work_mem`. Materialising
  liberally in a query run by fifty concurrent sessions is a memory
  incident waiting to happen.
- **Estimation above a fence is weak.** If a materialised CTE feeds a join
  whose order matters, expect the planner to guess. Sometimes the fix is to
  remove the fence you added.

## When not to use a CTE

- **When you need per-outer-row parameterisation.** A CTE is a standalone
  relation; it cannot reference the current row of the query using it. That
  is `LATERAL`, or a correlated subquery.
- **When the intermediate is reused across statements.** A CTE dies with the
  statement. If three queries need the same 200,000-row intermediate,
  build a temp table (and index it) or a materialized view.
- **When the "readability" is hiding a modelling problem.** A twelve-CTE
  query that recomputes the same joins in four steps is not architecture; it
  is a missing view or a missing table.
- **As a substitute for an index.** The most common failure mode in tuning
  work is restructuring a query five ways when the actual problem is a
  sequential scan on an unindexed foreign key.
- **In a hot OLTP path, blindly.** A materialised CTE inside a query that
  runs 2,000 times a second is 2,000 tuplestores a second.

## The architecture argument, restated

The reason to write pipelines rather than nests is not aesthetics; it is
**verifiability**. A five-step CTE query can be debugged by truncating it:
keep the `WITH` prefix, replace the final `SELECT` with `SELECT * FROM
step_three`, and look. Each step has a name that asserts its grain, and you
can check that assertion in isolation with a `count(*)` and a
`count(DISTINCT key)`. When a finance report disagrees with a spreadsheet,
this is how you find out which one is wrong, in minutes rather than an
afternoon.

Nested subqueries do not offer that. Neither does a single 200-line query
with nine joins and a `GROUP BY` over eleven columns, however clever. The
version a reviewer can check is the version that stays correct.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — name one step

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Finance wants revenue by customer country, over
**paid orders only**.

Put the population — paid orders — in a named CTE, then join `customers` in
the outer query. Columns, in this order:

1. `country`
2. `orders` — how many paid orders those customers placed
3. `revenue` — `sum(total)` of those orders

Any row order. There are twelve countries in `customers`, so expect at most
twelve rows.

The answer is identical if you filter in the outer `WHERE` instead. Write it
as a named step anyway, and notice what that does to how the query reads.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two grains, one join. The CTE's grain is "one row per paid order"; the
result's grain is "one row per country". The join to `customers` is what
carries you from the first to the second.

## Hint 2

The skeleton, with the interesting part left out:

```sql
WITH paid_orders AS (
    SELECT customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE ...
)
SELECT c.country, ...
FROM paid_orders p
JOIN customers c ON ...
GROUP BY c.country;
```

## Hint 3

Select only what you need inside the CTE — `customer_id` and `total`. The
outer query counts rows and sums totals, grouped by the country it got from
the join. Decide for yourself whether `count(*)` or `count(p.total)` is the
right spelling for `orders`, and be able to say why they could differ.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failure you are avoiding. If you join first and filter later,
a reviewer reading the query has to hold the whole join in their head before
they learn which orders count. Naming the population first means the second
half of the query is about one thing only: rolling up to country.

## Hint 2

Try writing it as a subquery first:

```sql
SELECT c.country, count(*), sum(p.total)
FROM (SELECT customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid') p
JOIN customers c ON c.id = p.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;
```

Now lift the parenthesised part out into a `WITH` and give it a name. The
plan will be identical — a single-reference CTE is inlined — so this really
is a pure refactoring.

## Hint 3

`total` is `NOT NULL` in this dataset, so `count(*)` and `count(p.total)`
agree. In a table where the column were nullable they would not, and
`count(*)` is the one that answers "how many orders". Pick it deliberately
rather than by habit.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex1 — name the population, then roll it up.
WITH paid_orders AS (
    SELECT customer_id, total
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'paid'
)
SELECT c.country,
       count(*)      AS orders,
       sum(p.total)  AS revenue
FROM paid_orders p
JOIN customers c ON c.id = p.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex1 — same answer, filtered after the join.
SELECT c.country,
       count(o.id)  AS orders,
       sum(o.total) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.country;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — a three-step pipeline

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Category revenue, built in three named steps so
that each one can be inspected on its own.

1. `line_revenue` — one row per line item on a non-cancelled order:
   `product_id` and `quantity * price`.
2. `product_revenue` — one row per product that sold anything.
3. the outer query — one row per category.

Columns, in this order:

1. `category`
2. `products` — how many distinct products in that category sold anything
3. `revenue` — total `sum(quantity * price)`

**Ordered by `revenue` descending.** Six rows, one per category.

`status <> 'cancelled'` throughout. Note that the middle step is where the
grain changes from "line" to "product" — that is the step you would run on
its own if the final numbers looked wrong.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write down the three grains before you write any SQL: one row per line item,
one row per product, one row per category. Each CTE is responsible for
exactly one of those transitions.

## Hint 2

The middle step is an ordinary `GROUP BY` over the first:

```sql
), product_revenue AS (
    SELECT product_id, sum(line_total) AS revenue
    FROM line_revenue
    GROUP BY product_id
)
```

Note it never mentions `orders` again — the population was settled in step
one.

## Hint 3

The outer query joins `product_revenue` to `products` to get the category,
then groups. `products` as a column name is `count(*)` at that point,
because `product_revenue` already has one row per product — that is what the
middle step bought you. Decide whether you still need `DISTINCT` anywhere,
and be able to justify the answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what happens if you skip the middle step and go straight from line items
to categories. The revenue is the same. The product count is not: over raw
line items you would need `count(DISTINCT product_id)`, which sorts or
hashes a million values. The pipeline turns that into a plain `count(*)`
over ten thousand rows.

## Hint 2

Debug it the way you would debug it in production. Write the `WITH` prefix,
then finish with:

```sql
SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT product_id) FROM line_revenue;
```

Those two numbers tell you whether step one has the grain you claimed. Then
swap the tail for `SELECT * FROM product_revenue LIMIT 5` and look again.

## Hint 3

Three CTEs referenced once each are all inlined, so this reads as three
paragraphs and plans as one query. If you want to see the difference, put
`AS MATERIALIZED` on the first one and compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`
output — a million-row tuplestore is a memorable thing to look at once.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex2 — line -> product -> category, named at each step.
WITH line_revenue AS (
    SELECT i.product_id,
           i.quantity * i.price AS line_total
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
), product_revenue AS (
    SELECT product_id,
           sum(line_total) AS revenue
    FROM line_revenue
    GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT p.category,
       count(*)          AS products,
       sum(pr.revenue)   AS revenue
FROM product_revenue pr
JOIN products p ON p.id = pr.product_id
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex2 — collapsed into one pass with a DISTINCT count.
SELECT p.category,
       count(DISTINCT i.product_id)   AS products,
       sum(i.quantity * i.price)      AS revenue
FROM order_items i
JOIN orders   o ON o.id = i.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — aggregate each side, then join

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The market overview, done without double counting.

For every customer `country`: how many customers we have there, how many
orders those customers have placed (any status), and their total revenue.
A country whose customers have never ordered must still appear, showing
zeros — not vanish.

Columns, in this order:

1. `country`
2. `customers`
3. `orders`
4. `revenue`

Any row order.

Build one CTE that counts customers per country from `customers` alone, a
second that counts and sums orders per country, and join them. Think about
which side must be the left side of the join, and put `coalesce` only where
it belongs.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are two independent questions here — "how many customers live there"
and "what did they buy" — and they have different populations. Answer each
one over its own rows, then line the answers up by country.

## Hint 2

The join direction is the whole exercise:

```sql
FROM customer_counts cc
LEFT JOIN order_stats os USING (country)
```

Every country has customers, so `customer_counts` is the complete list.
Not every country necessarily has orders, so `order_stats` is the side that
may be missing.

## Hint 3

`coalesce` goes on `os.orders` and `os.revenue`, never on `cc.country` — a
NULL country would mean your join is backwards, and hiding it with a default
would turn a bug into a plausible-looking row. Decide whether `revenue`
should coalesce to `0` or `0.00`, and whether that difference could matter
to a comparison.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the wrong version first, deliberately:

```sql
SELECT c.country, count(*), sum(o.total)
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.country;
```

Then ask what `count(*)` is counting. It is orders, not customers, because
the join already multiplied each customer by their order count. That is the
disease; this exercise is the cure.

## Hint 2

`count(DISTINCT c.id)` would patch the customer number — but it patches only
the number you noticed. Any customer with zero orders is still gone
entirely, because an inner join has no row for them. Two bugs, one join.

## Hint 3

Aggregating first also makes the join cheap: twelve rows against at most
twelve rows. Compare that with hashing half a million joined rows. Read the
two plans if you want the point to stick — the structural fix and the fast
fix are the same fix, which is not always true but is very satisfying when
it is.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex3 — two grains, aggregated apart, joined small.
WITH customer_counts AS (
    SELECT country, count(*) AS customers
    FROM customers
    GROUP BY country
), order_stats AS (
    SELECT c.country,
           count(*)      AS orders,
           sum(o.total)  AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.country
)
SELECT cc.country,
       cc.customers,
       coalesce(os.orders, 0)          AS orders,
       coalesce(os.revenue, 0)::numeric AS revenue
FROM customer_counts cc
LEFT JOIN order_stats os ON os.country = cc.country;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex3 — same shape via correlated scalar subqueries.
SELECT c.country,
       count(*) AS customers,
       (SELECT count(*)
        FROM orders o JOIN customers c2 ON c2.id = o.customer_id
        WHERE c2.country = c.country) AS orders,
       coalesce((SELECT sum(o.total)
                 FROM orders o JOIN customers c2 ON c2.id = o.customer_id
                 WHERE c2.country = c.country), 0)::numeric AS revenue
FROM customers c
GROUP BY c.country;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — reference the CTE twice

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Category revenue, with each category's share of the
whole business.

Columns, in this order:

1. `category`
2. `revenue` — `sum(quantity * price)` over `order_items` joined to
   `products`, all orders regardless of status
3. `pct` — `revenue` as a percentage of the total across all six
   categories, rounded to 2 decimal places

**Ordered by `revenue` descending.** Six rows.

Compute the per-category revenue **once**, in a CTE, then read that CTE
twice: once for the rows and once for the grand total. The six percentages
must add to 100.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The denominator is the sum of six numbers, not the sum of a million. Get the
six numbers first and the total becomes trivial — and cheap.

## Hint 2

A scalar subquery against your own CTE is the clean spelling:

```sql
SELECT category, revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / (SELECT sum(revenue) FROM cat), 2) AS pct
FROM cat
```

A window function over the CTE (`sum(revenue) OVER ()`) is the other correct
answer and reads about as well.

## Hint 3

Watch the types. `quantity` is `integer` and `price` is `numeric`, so
`quantity * price` is `numeric` and the division is exact — no `100.0`
trick needed here, unlike the integer-count case. Round at the end, not in
the middle, and check that your six percentages really do sum to 100.00
rather than 99.99.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is the exercise where the inlining rule becomes visible. Count your
references to the CTE: two. That means PostgreSQL will not inline it — it
will evaluate the aggregate once into a tuplestore and scan it twice. Which
is exactly what you want, and worth noticing that you got it for free.

## Hint 2

Confirm it rather than believing it:

```sql
EXPLAIN WITH cat AS (...) SELECT ... ;
```

Look for a `CTE Scan on cat` node and a `CTE cat` subplan. Then rewrite the
denominator as a second full aggregate over `order_items` — one reference
now — and watch both nodes disappear along with any hope of it being fast.

## Hint 3

`sum(revenue) OVER ()` computes the total across all rows of the window with
no partitioning, which here is all six categories. If you take that route,
remember the window function is evaluated after grouping, so it sees the six
grouped rows and not the raw line items. That is the same two-level idea ex6
will lean on much harder.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex4 — one aggregate, read twice: rows and total.
WITH cat AS (
    SELECT p.category,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT category,
       revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / (SELECT sum(revenue) FROM cat), 2) AS pct
FROM cat
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex4 — the total carried in by an empty-window sum.
SELECT category,
       revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / sum(revenue) OVER (), 2) AS pct
FROM (
    SELECT p.category,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
) c
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — the two-stage aggregate

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. How concentrated is our order volume? Produce the
distribution of orders per customer: for each order count, how many
customers placed exactly that many orders.

Columns, in this order:

1. `orders_per_customer`
2. `customers` — how many customers have exactly that many orders

**Ordered by `orders_per_customer` ascending.**

Only customers who placed at least one order appear (there is no row for
zero — you cannot count what `orders` does not contain; ex3's `LEFT JOIN` is
the tool if you ever need to).

Write the per-customer count as a CTE declared `AS MATERIALIZED`, and be
ready to say why that keyword changes the plan and not the answer.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are aggregating an aggregate. The first `GROUP BY` produces one row per
customer; the second groups those rows by the value the first computed.
`GROUP BY` alone cannot do that, because a query has one grouping level.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH per_customer AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT n AS orders_per_customer, count(*) AS customers
FROM per_customer
GROUP BY n
ORDER BY n;
```

That is nearly the whole answer — read it, then write your own and make sure
you can explain each line.

## Hint 3

`count(count(*))` is not legal SQL; PostgreSQL will tell you aggregate
function calls cannot be nested. The two-level structure — CTE or subquery,
either is fine — is the only way to express it. `AS MATERIALIZED` here is a
single-reference CTE that would otherwise be inlined; forcing the fence
gives you a tuplestore of one row per ordering customer, which you can see
in `EXPLAIN` as a `CTE Scan`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the answer looks like before you compute it. Orders are
spread over 50,000 customers, of whom about five thousand have none at all;
so the modal customer has a handful of orders and the tail is short. If your
result has one row with a gigantic count, you grouped by the wrong column.

## Hint 2

The same shape appears everywhere once you see it: reviews per product,
events per session, retries per request. All of them are "aggregate, then
histogram the aggregate", and all of them are two levels. A useful sanity
check is that `sum(customers)` across your result equals the number of
distinct `customer_id` values in `orders`.

## Hint 3

Try the exercise both ways — with `AS MATERIALIZED` and without — and
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` each. Same rows, different plan shape, and the
materialised one is not necessarily slower here because the intermediate is
small. That asymmetry is the lesson: the fence is a tool with a cost that
depends on the size of what you are fencing.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex5 — histogram of an aggregate, fenced on purpose.
WITH per_customer AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT n         AS orders_per_customer,
       count(*)  AS customers
FROM per_customer
GROUP BY n
ORDER BY n;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex5 — same two levels, spelled as a subquery.
SELECT pc.n AS orders_per_customer,
       count(*) AS customers
FROM (
    SELECT count(*) AS n
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
) pc
GROUP BY pc.n
ORDER BY pc.n;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the filter that must come after

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants the top three products in each
category by revenue, and — for each one — what share of its category's
revenue it represents.

Columns, in this order:

1. `category`
2. `product_id`
3. `revenue` — `sum(quantity * price)` for that product, all orders
4. `pct_of_category` — that revenue as a percentage of the category's
   **total** revenue across all its products, rounded to 2 decimals
5. `rn` — 1, 2 or 3

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `rn` ascending.** Eighteen rows.

Rank ties by `product_id` ascending so the answer is reproducible. The share
must be computed against every product in the category, not just the three
that survive — get this backwards and each row's `pct_of_category` will be
far too large.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two things have to happen in a fixed order: rank and total first, over the
whole category; keep only the top three second. A single query level cannot
do both, because you cannot filter on a window function in the same
`SELECT` that computes it.

## Hint 2

Both window calls live in the same CTE, over the grouped rows:

```sql
row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category
                   ORDER BY sum(i.quantity * i.price) DESC, i.product_id) AS rn,
sum(sum(i.quantity * i.price)) OVER (PARTITION BY p.category) AS cat_revenue
```

The doubled `sum` is not a typo: the inner one is the group's aggregate, the
outer one is a window over the grouped rows.

## Hint 3

The outer query then filters `WHERE rn <= 3` and divides `revenue` by
`cat_revenue`. If you instead compute the category total in the outer query
with `sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category)` after the filter, you will
get three-product totals and percentages near 100 — plausible enough to ship
and wrong. Decide where each number belongs before you type it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Recall the clause order: `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, windows,
`SELECT`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`. Windows are computed after grouping and
filtering. So the only place a window's output can be filtered is a level
above — which is precisely why "top N per group" is always two levels, in
every dialect.

## Hint 2

`DISTINCT ON` gives you the top *one* per group in a single level. It cannot
give you the top three, and it cannot give you a rank number. When the
requirement grows from 1 to N, `row_number()` plus an outer filter is the
shape that scales; recognising that moment is worth more than the syntax.

## Hint 3

Sanity-check the output: within each category the three `pct_of_category`
values should sum to something well under 100, because thousands of other
products in that category also sold. If they sum to exactly 100, you divided
by the wrong total.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex6 — rank and total over the whole group, filter above.
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT p.category,
           i.product_id,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category
                              ORDER BY sum(i.quantity * i.price) DESC,
                                       i.product_id) AS rn,
           sum(sum(i.quantity * i.price))
               OVER (PARTITION BY p.category) AS cat_revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category, i.product_id
)
SELECT category,
       product_id,
       revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / cat_revenue, 2) AS pct_of_category,
       rn
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category, rn;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex6 — per-product totals joined to a separate category total.
WITH prod AS (
    SELECT p.category, i.product_id,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category, i.product_id
), cat AS (
    SELECT category, sum(revenue) AS cat_revenue
    FROM prod
    GROUP BY category
), ranked AS (
    SELECT prod.*, cat.cat_revenue,
           rank() OVER (PARTITION BY prod.category
                        ORDER BY prod.revenue DESC, prod.product_id) AS rn
    FROM prod JOIN cat ON cat.category = prod.category
)
SELECT category, product_id, revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / cat_revenue, 2) AS pct_of_category,
       rn::bigint AS rn
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category, rn;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a data-modifying CTE

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Operations want to know the size of a backlog
before they act on it, and they want the number to come from the same
statement that touches the rows — not from a separate query that might race
with someone else's write.

Write a `WITH` clause containing an `UPDATE` over `orders` that touches
every row with `status = 'pending'` and `id <= 5000`, setting
`status = status`. That is deliberately a no-op on the value, so the
exercise is repeatable; PostgreSQL still writes a new row version for each
row, which is the honest cost of the pattern.

`RETURNING` the touched rows, then report from **the CTE**, not from
`orders`:

1. `rows_touched` — how many rows the `UPDATE` returned
2. `value` — `sum(total)` of those rows, rounded to 2 decimals

One row.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An `UPDATE` inside `WITH` behaves like any other CTE with one difference: it
produces rows only if you ask for them. `RETURNING` is that ask.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH touched AS (
    UPDATE some_table SET col = col
    WHERE ...
    RETURNING id, total
)
SELECT count(*) AS rows_touched, ... FROM touched;
```

The outer `SELECT` reads `touched`. It must not read `some_table`.

## Hint 3

Round with `round(sum(total), 2)`. Then try adding a second CTE that reads
`orders` with the same `WHERE` and see whether the two agree — they will
here, because the update does not change `status`, but reason about what
would happen if it did. That thought experiment is the whole point of the
exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it from the guarantee you are buying. Two statements — `UPDATE`
then `SELECT` — leave a window in which another session can change the rows
between them. One statement with a data-modifying CTE does not: the update
and the report are the same command, and the report is built from exactly
the rows the update touched.

## Hint 2

The real-world version of this shape is move-and-report:

```sql
WITH gone AS (DELETE FROM staging WHERE processed RETURNING *)
INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM gone;
```

Atomic, one snapshot, no intermediate state visible to anyone. Once you have
written that once, the pattern is yours.

## Hint 3

Remember the snapshot rule: sub-statements of one statement cannot see each
other's effects through a table. If you wrote a sibling
`SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped'` next to an `UPDATE`
that sets `status = 'shipped'`, the count would be the pre-update count, and
no amount of reordering the CTEs would change it. `RETURNING` is not a
convenience; it is the only door.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex7 — touch rows and report from RETURNING, one statement.
WITH touched AS (
    UPDATE orders
    SET status = status
    WHERE status = 'pending'
      AND id <= 5000
    RETURNING id, total
)
SELECT count(*)              AS rows_touched,
       round(sum(total), 2)  AS value
FROM touched;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex7 — the same population measured without writing.
SELECT count(*)              AS rows_touched,
       round(sum(total), 2)  AS value
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending'
  AND id <= 5000;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the long report

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The country scorecard, assembled from named steps.
Cancelled orders are excluded everywhere.

Columns, in this order:

1. `country`
2. `customers` — all customers registered in that country
3. `buyers` — customers there with at least one non-cancelled order
4. `revenue` — `sum(total)` of those orders
5. `aov` — `revenue / orders`, rounded to 2 decimals
6. `items_per_order` — line items on those orders divided by the number of
   those orders, rounded to 2 decimals

**Ordered by `revenue` descending.**

Every country has customers, so every country appears. Build it as separate
named steps — customers per country, order stats per country, line-item
counts per country — and join at the end. `aov` must be revenue over
*orders*, not the average of `total` over line-joined rows; those are
different numbers and only one is the average order value.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three grains again, and this time they are three different populations: all
customers, non-cancelled orders, line items on non-cancelled orders. Do not
let any of them touch another until each is aggregated to country.

## Hint 2

The middle step carries two numbers you will need twice:

```sql
), order_stats AS (
    SELECT c.country,
           count(*)                     AS orders,
           count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS buyers,
           sum(o.total)                 AS revenue
    FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY c.country
)
```

`orders` is the denominator of both `aov` and `items_per_order`.

## Hint 3

The line-item step joins `order_items` to `orders` to `customers` and counts
rows per country; nothing else, because that step must not contribute a sum
of `total` (that would be the fan-out bug wearing a disguise). Then a final
`SELECT` over all three with `LEFT JOIN` from the customer counts, dividing
where the prompt says to divide. Decide whether any `coalesce` is needed
here and justify your answer from the data.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by writing the five step names on a line, with nothing under them:
`customer_counts`, `order_stats`, `item_counts`, and the final select. If
those names do not read like a sentence describing the report, the
decomposition is wrong and the SQL will be too.

## Hint 2

`aov` is a trap with two spellings that look alike:

```sql
avg(o.total)                        -- correct, over order rows
avg(o.total) -- over o JOIN i ...   -- wrong: weights by line count
sum(o.total) / count(*)             -- correct, if count(*) counts orders
```

Because `order_stats` already carries `orders` and `revenue` at the right
grain, the division in the final `SELECT` cannot go wrong. That is the
architecture doing its job.

## Hint 3

Verify with an invariant, not by staring: `sum(buyers)` across your rows
must be at most `sum(customers)`, and `items_per_order` should sit somewhere
around two for this dataset since a million line items spread across half a
million orders. A value near one or near ten means a join went astray.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex8 — five named steps, joined once at the end.
WITH customer_counts AS (
    SELECT country, count(*) AS customers
    FROM customers
    GROUP BY country
), live_orders AS (
    SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.total, c.country
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
), order_stats AS (
    SELECT country,
           count(*)                    AS orders,
           count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS buyers,
           sum(total)                  AS revenue
    FROM live_orders
    GROUP BY country
), item_counts AS (
    SELECT lo.country, count(*) AS items
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN live_orders lo ON lo.id = i.order_id
    GROUP BY lo.country
)
SELECT cc.country,
       cc.customers,
       coalesce(os.buyers, 0)  AS buyers,
       coalesce(os.revenue, 0)::numeric AS revenue,
       round(os.revenue / os.orders, 2) AS aov,
       round(ic.items::numeric / os.orders, 2) AS items_per_order
FROM customer_counts cc
LEFT JOIN order_stats os ON os.country = cc.country
LEFT JOIN item_counts ic ON ic.country = cc.country
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / ex8 — the same report via scalar subqueries per country.
WITH live AS (
    SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.total, c.country
    FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
), base AS (
    SELECT c.country,
           count(*) AS customers,
           (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.customer_id) FROM live l
             WHERE l.country = c.country) AS buyers,
           (SELECT count(*) FROM live l WHERE l.country = c.country) AS orders,
           (SELECT sum(l.total) FROM live l WHERE l.country = c.country) AS revenue,
           (SELECT count(*) FROM order_items i
              JOIN live l ON l.id = i.order_id
             WHERE l.country = c.country) AS items
    FROM customers c
    GROUP BY c.country
)
SELECT country, customers, buyers, revenue::numeric AS revenue,
       round(revenue / orders, 2) AS aov,
       round(items::numeric / orders, 2) AS items_per_order
FROM base
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the best category per country

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. For every customer country, find the single
product category its customers spend the most on, and show how dominant that
category is.

Columns, in this order:

1. `country`
2. `category` — the winning category for that country
3. `category_revenue` — that category's line revenue in that country
4. `country_revenue` — the country's total line revenue across all
   categories
5. `pct` — `category_revenue` as a percentage of `country_revenue`, rounded
   to 2 decimals

**Ordered by `country` ascending.** Non-cancelled orders only. Break ties by
`category` ascending so the answer is reproducible.

This combines three things you have built separately: a pipeline that gets
line items to the (country, category) grain, a per-group top-1, and a total
computed at a coarser grain than the rows it decorates. Decide whether to
use `DISTINCT ON` or `row_number()`, and be able to defend the choice.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Get to one row per (country, category) first. Everything after that is
choosing a winner per country and attaching a country total — two problems
you have already solved in ex4 and ex6.

## Hint 2

The country total can ride along as a window over the grouped rows, so you
never need a second aggregate:

```sql
sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY country) AS country_revenue
```

computed in the same CTE that ranks. That leaves the outer query as a filter
and an arithmetic expression.

## Hint 3

`DISTINCT ON (country) ... ORDER BY country, revenue DESC, category` is the
compact spelling and gives you the winner directly, but note that
`DISTINCT ON` is applied after window functions, so a window computed in the
same level is still evaluated over all rows — which is what you want here.
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY revenue DESC, category)`
plus `WHERE rn = 1` in an outer level is the spelling that generalises to
top-N. Pick one and say why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Work out the grain chain on paper: `order_items` (one row per line) →
join `orders` and `customers` for country, join `products` for category →
`GROUP BY country, category` (one row per pair) → pick one per country.
Four grains, and the errors all live at the transitions.

## Hint 2

A different route to the same answer avoids windows entirely: build the
(country, category) revenue CTE, build a per-country max CTE from it, then
join them on `country` and `revenue = max_revenue`. It is correct, and it
has a bug waiting — if two categories tie at the maximum, the join yields
both and the country appears twice. That is why the prompt insists on a
tie-break; whichever route you take, the tie-break has to be somewhere.

## Hint 3

Check the result the way a reviewer would: `pct` should be comfortably above
100/6 ≈ 16.7 for most countries if categories are unevenly loved there, and
close to it if they are not. Twelve rows out, one per country, no
duplicates — run `SELECT country, count(*) FROM (your query) q GROUP BY 1
HAVING count(*) > 1` and confirm it is empty.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / challenge — top category per country with its share.
WITH line_country AS (
    SELECT c.country, p.category,
           i.quantity * i.price AS line_total
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN orders    o ON o.id = i.order_id
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    JOIN products  p ON p.id = i.product_id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
), by_pair AS (
    SELECT country, category, sum(line_total) AS category_revenue
    FROM line_country
    GROUP BY country, category
), decorated AS (
    SELECT country, category, category_revenue,
           sum(category_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY country) AS country_revenue,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country
                              ORDER BY category_revenue DESC, category) AS rn
    FROM by_pair
)
SELECT country, category, category_revenue, country_revenue,
       round(100 * category_revenue / country_revenue, 2) AS pct
FROM decorated
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY country;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / challenge — DISTINCT ON for the winner, join for the total.
WITH by_pair AS (
    SELECT c.country, p.category,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS category_revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN orders    o ON o.id = i.order_id
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    JOIN products  p ON p.id = i.product_id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY c.country, p.category
), totals AS (
    SELECT country, sum(category_revenue) AS country_revenue
    FROM by_pair GROUP BY country
), winner AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (country) country, category, category_revenue
    FROM by_pair
    ORDER BY country, category_revenue DESC, category
)
SELECT w.country, w.category, w.category_revenue, t.country_revenue,
       round(100 * w.category_revenue / t.country_revenue, 2) AS pct
FROM winner w
JOIN totals t ON t.country = w.country
ORDER BY w.country;

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — orders versus lines

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. For each product category: how many **distinct
orders** contained at least one product from it, and the total line revenue
from that category.

Columns, in this order:

1. `category`
2. `orders` — distinct orders containing at least one line in that category
3. `revenue` — `sum(quantity * price)` for that category

Any row order. All orders regardless of status. Six rows.

One of these two numbers is easy and one has a trap in it. An order
containing three books produces three `order_items` rows, so `count(*)` over
that join counts lines, not orders. Name the grain you are at before you
choose the aggregate.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f01_cte_architecture review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The join `order_items × products` has one row per line item. Revenue is a
sum over lines and is therefore correct as written. "How many orders" is a
question about a coarser grain and needs to say so.

## Hint 2

```sql
count(DISTINCT i.order_id) AS orders,
sum(i.quantity * i.price)  AS revenue
```

Both aggregates read the same rows; only the first one has to un-duplicate.

## Hint 3

There is a second, structural answer: reduce to one row per (order,
category) in a CTE first, then `count(*)` at that grain and sum the
per-pair revenue. It costs more lines and it is what you would reach for if
the requirement grew to "and the average number of lines per order per
category". Try both and compare the plans.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what a reader would do with `orders`. If they intend to divide revenue
by it to get "revenue per order in this category", then it must count orders
— and if the query counts lines instead, the resulting number will look
reasonable and be about half of the truth. Wrong reports usually pass the
smell test; that is what makes them expensive.

## Hint 2

`count(DISTINCT ...)` is honest but not free: it sorts or hashes the whole
column per group. For six groups over a million rows it is fine. For a
million groups it is the thing that makes the report time out, and the
CTE-first restructuring is what you would switch to.

## Hint 3

An order can contain products from several categories, so summing `orders`
across the six rows will exceed the number of orders in the table. That is
correct, not a bug — but if a stakeholder adds up your column and asks why
it exceeds the order count, you should have the sentence ready before they
ask it.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / review1 — two aggregates, two grains, one pass.
SELECT p.category,
       count(DISTINCT i.order_id)  AS orders,
       sum(i.quantity * i.price)   AS revenue
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
GROUP BY p.category;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f01_cte_architecture / review1 — collapse to (order, category) first, then count.
WITH per_order_category AS (
    SELECT i.order_id, p.category,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY i.order_id, p.category
)
SELECT category,
       count(*)      AS orders,
       sum(revenue)  AS revenue
FROM per_order_category
GROUP BY category;

lessons.title: V3·F2 — Recursive CTEs: hierarchies, graphs and generated series
lessons.summary: Lesson 14 gave you base case, UNION ALL, step. This one is about what the executor really runs, why the recursive reference may appear exactly once, how a cycle in the data turns a query into an outage, and the SEARCH and CYCLE clauses that make ordering and cycle detection declarative.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·F2 — Recursive CTEs: hierarchies, graphs and generated series

Lesson 14 showed you the skeleton and pointed it at the org chart. It worked,
and it probably felt like magic. This sector removes the magic. Recursion in
SQL is a small, completely mechanical loop over a **working table**, and once
you can describe that loop out loud, every hierarchy and graph question in
the language collapses into the same five lines with one join swapped.

It also removes the danger. A recursive CTE against real data with a cycle in
it does not return a wrong answer; it runs until it fills a disk. Knowing how
to guard one is not advanced material. It is the entry fee.

## Concept

The syntax is `WITH RECURSIVE name AS (base UNION ALL step)`, and the
execution is this, exactly:

1. Evaluate the **base term** once. Its rows go into the result and into a
   *working table*.
2. Evaluate the **recursive term**, with `name` bound to the working table
   only — not the whole result so far.
3. Append those rows to the result; they become the new working table.
4. Repeat from 2 until an iteration produces zero rows.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth
    FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL          -- base: the CEO
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, org.depth + 1
    FROM staff s
    JOIN org ON s.manager_id = org.id            -- step: one edge down
)
SELECT * FROM org;
```

Three restrictions follow directly from that loop, and PostgreSQL enforces
all of them. The recursive reference may appear **exactly once**; it may not
sit on the nullable side of an outer join; and it may not appear inside a
subquery or under an aggregate. You cannot aggregate the working table
mid-flight, because the working table is not the answer — it is the frontier.

**`UNION` versus `UNION ALL`.** `UNION` deduplicates the accumulated result
each round. That makes a cyclic graph terminate — eventually every node has
been seen — at the cost of a sort or hash per iteration. But it only saves
you if the rows repeat *exactly*. Carry a `depth` column and `(node, 1)` and
`(node, 2)` are different rows, so the loop runs forever anyway. This catches
people constantly.

**Cycle guards.** The portable one is a visited list:

```sql
    SELECT e.dst, t.path || e.dst
    FROM edges e JOIN t ON e.src = t.node
    WHERE NOT e.dst = ANY(t.path)
```

Since PostgreSQL 14 there is a declarative one:

```sql
) CYCLE node SET is_cycle USING path
```

which adds two columns — a boolean flag and the path array — and stops
expanding a branch when a node repeats. The `SEARCH` clause is its sibling:
`SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord` builds a sortable array you can
`ORDER BY` to get true tree order, and `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET ord`
gives you level order instead.

**Direction is one join.** `ON s.manager_id = t.id` walks down (my subtree).
`ON s.id = t.manager_id` walks up (my managers). Same five lines.

**Recursion is not only for trees.** A `VALUES` list is a perfectly good
graph, a series is a recursion whose step is arithmetic, and any computation
where the next state depends on the previous state — and only on it — is a
recursive CTE. For plain integer and timestamp series, `generate_series()`
is faster and clearer; use recursion when the step is data-dependent.

## Exercise 1 — the org chart, and the version without recursion

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Every staff member with their depth: the CEO is 1,
her direct reports 2, and so on. Columns: `id`, `name`, `depth`. All 500
rows, any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex1`

## Exercise 2 — one person's subtree

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Employee **2** and everyone who reports to them,
directly or indirectly. Columns: `id`, `name`, `depth` — employee 2 is depth
1. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex2`

## Exercise 3 — the chain upward

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Employee **442**'s management chain, from
themselves up to the CEO. Columns: `pos` (1 = employee 442), `id`, `name`.
**Ordered by `pos` ascending.** The tree is four levels deep, so this is a
short result.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex3`

## Exercise 4 — a materialized path

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Every staff member with a path string built during
the recursion: `/1`, `/1/17`, `/1/17/93`. Columns: `id`, `name`, `depth`,
`path`. **Ordered by `path` ascending** — which puts each subtree together,
because that is what a path sorts like.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex4`

## Exercise 5 — rolling up a subtree

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. For every employee: how many people are in their
subtree including themselves, and the total salary of that subtree. Columns:
`id`, `name`, `subtree_staff`, `subtree_payroll`. **Ordered by `id`
ascending.** All 500 rows; a leaf's subtree is just themselves.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex5`

## Exercise 6 — a graph with a cycle in it

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Define this directed graph inline with `VALUES` —
`a→b`, `a→g`, `b→c`, `g→c`, `c→d`, `d→b`, `c→e`, `e→f`, `f→a` — and return
every node reachable from `a`, including `a` itself. One column, `node`,
**ordered ascending**, each node once. Seven rows.

`d→b` and `f→a` are cycles. A naive recursion never terminates; guard it.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex6`

## Exercise 7 — shortest hops, declaratively

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Same graph. For every reachable node, the **fewest
hops** from `a`. Columns: `node`, `hops` (`a` is 0). **Ordered by `node`.**

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex7`

## Exercise 8 — a step the data decides

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The Collatz sequence from 27: halve if even, else
triple and add one, until you reach 1. Columns: `step` (0 for the starting
value), `n`. **Ordered by `step` ascending.** The first row is `(0, 27)` and
the last row's `n` is 1.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex8`

## Challenge — the top earner at every level

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Combine the depth recursion with a window:
for each depth in the org tree, the single highest-paid person at that
depth. Columns: `depth`, `id`, `name`, `salary`. Ties broken by `id`
ascending. **Ordered by `depth` ascending.**

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: the leaves. Every staff member who manages nobody, with their
depth. Columns: `id`, `name`, `depth`. Any order.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3f02_recursive_ctes

A recursive CTE is a loop with a fixed shape, and the whole skill is being
able to say what is in the working table at each turn. Everything else —
cycles, ordering, closures, series — is a consequence.

## Notes

**The working table is the frontier, not the result.** Round *n* of the
recursive term sees only the rows round *n-1* produced. That is why depth
arithmetic works (`t.depth + 1` is always the previous level), why you cannot
aggregate over the CTE inside itself (there is nothing complete to aggregate),
and why the reference may appear only once — there is one working table, and
joining it to itself would need two.

**Termination is a property of your step, not of the language.** The loop
stops when an iteration yields no rows. In a tree that happens naturally: at
the deepest level, no staff row has a `manager_id` in the frontier. In a
graph with a cycle it never happens, and PostgreSQL will keep going until
temp space runs out. There is no automatic depth limit.

**`UNION` deduplicates; that is weaker than it sounds.** It compares whole
rows. `(b, 1)` and `(b, 3)` are distinct, so the moment you carry a depth or
a path the deduplication stops protecting you. Only a guard that looks at the
*node* — a visited array, or the `CYCLE` clause — actually cuts the loop.

**`CYCLE` and `SEARCH` are PostgreSQL 14+ sugar over things you can hand-roll.**
`CYCLE node SET is_cycle USING path` maintains the visited array for you,
marks the row that closed the loop, and stops expanding it. `SEARCH DEPTH
FIRST BY id SET ord` builds an array of the `id` values along the path so
`ORDER BY ord` gives you tree order; `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET ord`
builds `(depth, id)` pairs so the same `ORDER BY` gives level order. Neither
changes which rows you get, only how they are labelled and ordered.

**Recursion produces rows in no guaranteed order.** It happens to come out
breadth-first because of how the working table is refilled, but that is an
implementation detail and not a contract. If order matters, carry something
sortable — a counter, a path array, a materialized path string — or use
`SEARCH`.

**Upward and downward are one join apart.** `s.manager_id = t.id` descends;
`s.id = t.manager_id` ascends. Multiple roots in the base term is fine, and
is how you do "the subtrees of these forty managers" in one pass.

**Transitive closure explodes.** A `(root, node)` closure over a 500-row,
4-level tree is small. Over a dense graph it is quadratic in the node count,
and over a cyclic one with a path guard it is the number of *simple paths* —
which is factorial-ish. Always know which of those three you are in.

**`generate_series` beats recursion for regular series.** Integers, dates,
timestamps with a fixed step: use the function. It is a set-returning
function that streams, with no working table and no per-round overhead.
Recursion earns its place when the next value depends on the current one in
a way arithmetic cannot express in closed form.

## ex1 — the org chart

What this tested: the canonical five lines. The classic mistake is joining
`org` to `staff` in the wrong direction and getting only the CEO back,
because no row satisfies `s.id = org.manager_id` when `org` holds the root.
The reference answer's alternative — four `UNION ALL`ed self-joins — is worth
reading precisely because it is correct here and unmaintainable: it hard-codes
the knowledge that the tree is four deep, and a fifth level would appear as
silently missing rows.

## ex2 — one person's subtree

What this tested: that the base term chooses the roots. Nothing else changes.
The classic mistake is filtering in the outer query instead — `WHERE depth >
1 AND ...` over the full org chart — which computes 500 rows to keep a
handful and cannot express "relative depth" at all.

## ex3 — the chain upward

What this tested: the reversed join, plus the fact that recursion has no
inherent order, so `pos` must be computed inside. The classic mistake is
`ORDER BY id` and hoping — ids are not depth. The reference alternative
computes the same chain by descending from the CEO with a path array and
then unnesting `WITH ORDINALITY`, which is a good trick to have seen.

## ex4 — a materialized path

What this tested: accumulating state through the recursion. A path is just a
column that concatenates instead of adding. Sorting by it gives depth-first
order for free — with one caveat worth knowing: string paths sort
lexicographically, so `/1/10` precedes `/1/9`. Zero-padding or an integer
array fixes that when it matters.

## ex5 — rolling up a subtree

What this tested: turning a tree into a `(root, descendant)` closure and then
aggregating it like any ordinary table. The base term pairs every node with
itself — that is what makes a leaf's subtree contain the leaf. The classic
mistake is starting the closure only at the CEO, which produces one root and
one giant subtree.

## ex6 — a graph with a cycle in it

What this tested: whether you guard before you run. The `VALUES` graph is
deliberately tiny so that a runaway recursion is obvious rather than fatal.
Both correct answers — the `path` array with `NOT node = ANY(path)`, and the
`CYCLE` clause — do the same thing; the array version works on PostgreSQL 13
and older, which is still a lot of production.

## ex7 — shortest hops

What this tested: that carrying a changing column defeats `UNION`'s
deduplication, so the guard has to be explicit *and* the minimum has to be
taken afterwards. The recursion enumerates simple paths; `min(hops)` per node
collapses them to the shortest. `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST` gives the same answer
by construction, which is the more elegant route.

## ex8 — a step the data decides

What this tested: recursion as iteration. There is no closed form for the
Collatz step, no `generate_series` that produces it, and no window function
that can — the next value is a function of the previous value, which is
exactly the case SQL's recursion exists for. The classic mistake is putting
the stopping condition in the outer query instead of the recursive term,
which never terminates because the loop keeps generating 1, 4, 2, 1, 4, 2.

## challenge — the top earner at every level

What this tested: recursion feeding a window function. Once the CTE has
produced `depth`, the rest is a per-partition top-1 — `DISTINCT ON` or
`row_number()`, either is fine — and the tie-break has to be explicit or the
answer is not reproducible.

## review1 — the leaves

The anti-join angle: a leaf is a staff row that appears in nobody's
`manager_id`. `NOT EXISTS` is the clearest spelling; `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL`
and `NOT IN` both work, and `NOT IN` is the one that breaks if the column
ever contains a NULL — which `manager_id` does, for the CEO. That is not a
hypothetical here; it is the first row in the table.

## Further reading

- [`WITH` Queries — recursive](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — the working-table algorithm written out, plus the `SEARCH` and `CYCLE` clauses and the cycle-detection example.
- [`SELECT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the exact restrictions on where the recursive self-reference may appear.
- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — `generate_series` for numbers and timestamps, and `unnest ... WITH ORDINALITY`.
- [Array Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-array.html) — `= ANY(array)`, `||`, and `array_to_string`, the building blocks of a hand-rolled cycle guard.
- [`VALUES` Lists](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-values.html) — building a relation inline, which is how you test graph queries without a table.

# V3·F2 — Recursive CTEs: hierarchies, graphs and generated series

The archive version: the loop, the guards, the clauses, and the shapes.

## 1. The algorithm, spelled out

```
result    := {}
working   := evaluate(base_term)
result    += working
loop:
    next  := evaluate(recursive_term with CTE bound to `working`)
    exit when next is empty
    result  += next
    working := next
```

With `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL`, `next` is first deduplicated against
`result` before both appends.

Everything about recursive CTEs falls out of this:

- **One reference.** There is one `working` table per iteration, so the
  recursive term may mention the CTE exactly once. `t JOIN t` is rejected.
- **No outer-join nullable side.** A `LEFT JOIN t` would require rows for the
  absence of frontier rows, which the loop cannot express.
- **No aggregates or subqueries over the self-reference.** `sum()` over
  `working` would aggregate a frontier, not a result — meaningless.
- **No `ORDER BY`/`LIMIT` in the recursive term.** Same reason.

## 2. Trees

```sql
-- descendants of node X, with relative depth
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth FROM staff WHERE id = 2
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, sub.depth + 1
    FROM staff s JOIN sub ON s.manager_id = sub.id
)
SELECT * FROM sub;

-- ancestors of node X
WITH RECURSIVE up AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS pos FROM staff WHERE id = 442
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, up.pos + 1
    FROM staff s JOIN up ON s.id = up.manager_id
)
SELECT pos, id, name FROM up ORDER BY pos;
```

The base term picks the roots; the join direction picks up or down. Multiple
roots in the base term is fine and costs nothing extra.

### Paths

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth, '/' || id AS path
    FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, t.depth + 1, t.path || '/' || s.id
    FROM staff s JOIN tree t ON s.manager_id = t.id
)
SELECT * FROM tree ORDER BY path;
```

Text paths sort lexicographically (`/1/10` < `/1/9`); integer arrays sort
element-wise and do not have that problem. Use `ARRAY[id]` and `t.path ||
s.id` when order matters, text when human readability does.

### Transitive closure and roll-ups

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE closure AS (
    SELECT id AS root, id AS node, salary FROM staff
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.root, s.id, s.salary
    FROM closure c JOIN staff s ON s.manager_id = c.node
)
SELECT root, count(*) AS n, sum(salary) AS payroll
FROM closure GROUP BY root;
```

The base term pairs each node with itself, so every node's closure includes
itself and leaves come out with `n = 1`. Note the size: a closure over a
4-level tree of 500 nodes has roughly 500 × average-depth rows. Over a wide,
deep hierarchy it is the thing that eats your `work_mem`.

## 3. Graphs

Trees terminate for free. Graphs do not.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE edges(src, dst) AS (
    VALUES ('a','b'), ('b','c'), ('c','d'), ('d','b')
),
walk AS (
    SELECT 'a'::text AS node, ARRAY['a'::text] AS path
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.dst, w.path || e.dst
    FROM walk w JOIN edges e ON e.src = w.node
    WHERE NOT e.dst = ANY(w.path)            -- the guard
)
SELECT DISTINCT node FROM walk ORDER BY node;
```

Three guard strategies, in order of preference:

1. **Visited array.** Correct, portable, and the array is useful output.
   Cost: the array grows with depth and comparison is O(depth).
2. **`CYCLE` clause** (PG 14+). Same semantics, less typing, and the
   `is_cycle` flag tells you *where* the cycle is:
   ```sql
   ) CYCLE node SET is_cycle USING path
   ```
3. **Depth cap.** `WHERE depth < 20`. Not a correctness guard — it is a
   circuit breaker. Add it anyway on untrusted data; a wrong answer that
   returns beats a right answer that never does.

`UNION` (not `ALL`) works *only* if the rows repeat exactly. As soon as you
carry depth, a path, or a running cost, it stops helping.

### Shortest path

The recursion enumerates simple paths; take the minimum afterwards:

```sql
SELECT node, min(cardinality(path) - 1) AS hops
FROM walk GROUP BY node;
```

Or let `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY node SET ord` order the result and take the
first row per node with `DISTINCT ON`.

## 4. Series and iteration

```sql
-- don't
WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i+1 FROM n WHERE i < 12)
SELECT i FROM n;
-- do
SELECT i FROM generate_series(1, 12) AS i;
-- also do: timestamps
SELECT d FROM generate_series(timestamptz '2023-10-01',
                              timestamptz '2023-11-01',
                              interval '1 day') AS d;
```

Recursion wins when the step is data-dependent:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE collatz(step, n) AS (
    SELECT 0, 27
    UNION ALL
    SELECT step + 1, CASE WHEN n % 2 = 0 THEN n / 2 ELSE 3 * n + 1 END
    FROM collatz WHERE n <> 1
)
SELECT * FROM collatz ORDER BY step;
```

Note where the stop condition lives: **in the recursive term**. Putting it in
the outer query does not stop the loop; the loop is what has to stop.

## 5. Common mistakes

- Joining the wrong way and getting only the base rows back.
- Carrying `depth` and expecting `UNION` to break the cycle.
- Putting the termination condition in the outer `SELECT`.
- Aggregating inside the recursive term (rejected) or expecting the CTE to
  see its own complete result (it sees the frontier).
- Assuming output order. It is not specified; carry a sort key.
- Building a closure over a graph without a guard and blaming the database.
- Using recursion where `generate_series` does the job faster.
- `NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM staff)` for "leaves" — `manager_id` is NULL
  for the CEO and `NOT IN` with a NULL returns no rows at all.

## 6. The interview answer

> *"How does a recursive CTE actually execute?"*

"It is not recursion in the function-call sense — it is iteration over a
working table. The base term runs once and its rows become the working table.
Then the recursive term runs with the CTE name bound to just that working
table, its output is appended to the result and becomes the new working
table, and it repeats until an iteration returns nothing. That is why the
self-reference can appear only once and can't be aggregated over, why
`UNION` deduplicates per round while `UNION ALL` doesn't, and why cycles
never terminate unless you carry a visited set — or use the `CYCLE` clause in
14 and up. For ordering I use `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST` or carry a path array,
because the output order isn't guaranteed."

## Check yourself

1. Describe the working-table loop in four steps without looking.
2. Why may the recursive self-reference appear exactly once?
3. Give a case where `UNION` breaks a cycle and a case where it does not.
4. Write the guard predicate for a visited-array cycle check.
5. What two things does `CYCLE node SET flag USING path` add to your rows?
6. What does `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET ord` put in `ord`, and how do
   you use it?
7. Change one token in a descendants query to make it an ancestors query.
8. How large is the `(root, node)` closure of a balanced tree with N nodes
   and depth D? Why is that different for a dense graph?
9. Why do text materialized paths sort `/1/10` before `/1/9`, and what fixes
   it?
10. When is recursion the right tool for a series, and when is
    `generate_series` obviously better?
11. Where must the Collatz stopping condition go, and what happens if you put
    it in the outer query?
12. Why does `NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM staff)` return zero rows on this
    dataset?
13. You need "the subtrees of these forty managers, each with relative
    depth". What changes?

# The long read — iteration in a language that has no loops

## Where it came from

SQL was designed without iteration on purpose. The relational model is a
calculus over sets, and the whole selling point in 1974 was that you declared
*what* you wanted and left *how* to the system. Iteration is a "how". For two
decades the standard answer to "how do I query a hierarchy" was either
"denormalise it" (nested sets, materialized paths, closure tables — all still
excellent techniques) or "write a cursor loop in the application".

Oracle shipped `CONNECT BY` in the 1980s, a proprietary hierarchy operator
that solved the tree case and only the tree case. The SQL:1999 committee took
a different route and defined **recursive common table expressions** — a
general fixed-point iteration that happens to solve trees, and also graphs,
series, string splitting, and anything else expressible as "repeat this
relational step until nothing new appears". PostgreSQL implemented it in 8.4
(2009); SQL Server had it in 2005; MySQL, remarkably, waited until 8.0
(2018).

The generality is the point. `CONNECT BY` cannot compute a Collatz sequence
or a shortest path over an arbitrary edge list. A recursive CTE can, because
its step is an arbitrary query.

## What the executor builds

PostgreSQL's plan for a recursive CTE is a `Recursive Union` node with two
children: the base plan and the recursive plan. The recursive plan contains a
`WorkTable Scan` node — the physical representation of "the rows produced by
the previous iteration".

At run time the executor keeps two tuplestores, conventionally called the
working table and the intermediate table. It runs the recursive plan with the
`WorkTable Scan` reading the working table, collects output into the
intermediate table, and when the recursive plan is exhausted it swaps them
and goes again. The loop ends when a swap produces an empty working table.

This is why the restrictions are what they are. There is exactly one
`WorkTable Scan` slot, so exactly one self-reference. The working table is
consumed by a scan, so it cannot sit under an aggregate that needs the whole
relation, nor on the nullable side of an outer join, which would need to
produce rows in the absence of scan output. With `UNION` rather than `UNION
ALL`, the node also maintains a hash table of everything emitted so far and
filters the intermediate table against it each round — which is where the
cost of deduplication lives.

Estimation is the weak spot. The planner has to guess how many iterations
will happen and how many rows each produces; historically it assumes a small
constant factor. A recursive CTE that fans out hard will be badly estimated,
and everything joined above it will be planned on those bad numbers. If a
recursive query is slow, check whether the *recursion* is slow or whether a
join above it chose a nested loop on an estimate of ten rows when the real
answer was ten million.

## The safety story

There is no automatic iteration limit. A cyclic graph plus an unguarded
recursion runs until temporary files fill the filesystem, and because the
work happens inside one statement, an idle-transaction timeout will not save
you. `statement_timeout` will, which is a good argument for setting it on
anything analytical.

Three defences, and you should think of them as layered rather than
alternative:

1. A **visited set** — the array guard, or the `CYCLE` clause — makes the
   query correct on cyclic data.
2. A **depth cap** makes it *terminate* even if your guard has a bug. On
   untrusted or externally-loaded graph data, add one.
3. A **statement timeout** makes it terminate even if both of the above are
   wrong.

The `CYCLE` clause deserves a note on its semantics: it does not merely stop:
it emits the row that closed the cycle, with `is_cycle` set true, and then
declines to expand it. That means you can *report* cycles — "these forty
manager records form a reporting loop" — which is exactly what a data-quality
job wants, rather than silently pruning them.

## Performance notes

- **Closures are quadratic-ish.** A `(root, node)` closure over a tree of N
  nodes with average depth D has about N × D rows. That is fine at 500 × 3.
  At ten million nodes it is not a query, it is a table you should have
  maintained incrementally.
- **The array guard is O(depth) per row comparison.** Deep paths get slower
  per step. For very deep walks, a `bit` or hash-based visited representation
  is a real optimisation, at the cost of readability.
- **Indexes matter enormously.** Every iteration runs the step query. A
  descendants walk does one lookup per frontier row on `staff.manager_id`;
  without an index on that column, every iteration is a sequential scan of
  the whole table. In this dataset there is no such index (the template has
  none beyond primary keys), which is why a 500-row tree is instant and a
  500,000-row one would not be.
- **`generate_series` is not a recursion.** It is a set-returning function
  that streams values with no tuplestore and no per-round plan execution. For
  regular series it is not slightly faster; it is a different order of
  magnitude.
- **Materialisation is mandatory.** Recursive CTEs are never inlined, so
  their output is always stored. Selecting five columns instead of `*` from a
  wide table is a real saving here in a way it is not for an inlined CTE.

## When not to use it

- **When the hierarchy is read a thousand times more often than it changes.**
  Maintain a closure table or a materialized path column with triggers and
  make the read a plain indexed lookup. Recursion at query time is the
  general answer, not always the right one.
- **When the depth is fixed and small and known forever.** Three explicit
  joins are clearer than a recursion for a rigid three-level category tree —
  though "known forever" is a claim that ages badly.
- **When you want a regular series.** `generate_series`.
- **When the step needs to see the whole result so far.** A recursive CTE
  cannot: the frontier is not the result. Running totals over an ordered
  sequence are window functions, not recursion, and the window version is
  vastly faster.
- **When the graph is genuinely large and you need real graph algorithms.**
  Weighted shortest paths, centrality, community detection — SQL can express
  Dijkstra-ish things awkwardly, but a graph database or an in-memory
  algorithm will beat it by orders of magnitude. Knowing where the boundary
  is matters more than being able to cross it.

There is one more boundary worth naming: recursion inside a transaction that
also writes. A recursive CTE holds its tuplestores for the life of the
statement, and a long walk over a large hierarchy can hold a snapshot open
for minutes. On a busy cluster that delays vacuum's ability to reclaim dead
tuples across the whole database, so a slow analytical recursion is not only
slow for the person who ran it. Run these against a replica when you have
one, and set a statement timeout when you do not.

## The habit worth building

Before writing any recursive CTE, answer three questions in a comment above
it: what is in the base term, what one edge does the step follow, and what
makes the step eventually return nothing. If the third answer is "the data is
a tree", write down what happens the day it is not. That comment is the
difference between a query that fails loudly on bad data and one that takes
the cluster down at 3 a.m.

## Exercise 1 — the org chart, and the version without recursion

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Every staff member with their depth in the
reporting tree. The CEO — the only row with `manager_id IS NULL` — is depth
1, her direct reports are depth 2, and so on.

Columns, in this order:

1. `id`
2. `name`
3. `depth`

All 500 rows, any row order.

Type the recursion rather than pasting it, and before you run it, say out
loud why the loop stops. The reference answer's second spelling — four
`UNION ALL`ed self-joins — is correct only because someone told you the tree
is four levels deep; that is the difference the recursion buys.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f02_recursive_ctes ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two questions decide the whole query: which rows start the walk, and which
single edge does each step follow. The root is the row with no manager. The
edge is "s is managed by someone already in the result".

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth
    FROM staff
    WHERE ...
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, org.depth + 1
    FROM staff s
    JOIN org ON ...
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM org;
```

## Hint 3

The join condition is `s.manager_id = org.id` — new rows are the people
managed by rows already found. Write it the other way round and the first
iteration returns nothing, because no staff row has an `id` equal to the
CEO's `manager_id` (which is NULL). That failure mode is instant and
diagnostic: an empty second level means the arrow is backwards.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Simulate the loop on paper for the first two rounds. Round 0: the working
table holds one row, the CEO, depth 1. Round 1: the step joins `staff` to
that one row and finds everyone whose `manager_id` is the CEO's id, depth 2.
Round 2: the step sees only those depth-2 rows. If you can narrate that, the
SQL writes itself.

## Hint 2

Ask what would happen with `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL` here. Nothing —
the rows are all distinct because ids are unique, so deduplication finds
nothing to remove and you pay for a hash per round. In a tree, `UNION ALL`
is always the right choice.

## Hint 3

Compare your row count against 500. If you get fewer, some subtree is
unreachable — which in this data would mean an orphan whose manager does not
exist. If you get more, you have a cycle or a duplicate join key. Both are
data-quality findings worth more than the query itself.

WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth
    FROM staff
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, org.depth + 1
    FROM staff s
    JOIN org ON s.manager_id = org.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth
FROM org;
