## Exercise 1 — the missing days

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Daily review counts for **product 42** during
October 2023, computed the obvious way.

Columns, in this order:

1. `day` — the UTC calendar day, as a `date`
2. `reviews`

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** Half-open range:
`created_at >= '2023-10-01 00:00+00'` and `< '2023-11-01 00:00+00'`.

Derive the day with `(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date` rather than
`date_trunc('day', created_at)` — the second one truncates in whatever time
zone the session happens to be set to, and this course's answers have to be
the same on every machine.

Count the rows when it returns. There are fewer than 31, and that is the
entire point of the exercise: this is the report before it is correct.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An ordinary grouped count. The only decisions are how you name the bucket
and how you write the date range.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day, count(*) AS reviews
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42
  AND created_at >= timestamptz '2023-10-01 00:00+00'
  AND created_at <  timestamptz '2023-11-01 00:00+00'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

## Hint 3

Note the explicit `+00` on the literals. Without it, a bare string is
interpreted in the session time zone, so the window's edges move with the
reader — the same class of bug as the un-zoned `date_trunc`. Once it runs,
decide what you would tell a stakeholder who asked why one of the days is
missing from the chart.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the output rather than the query. You are producing a series
that will be plotted. Ask, before you write anything, how many points it
should contain. Thirty-one is the answer the reader assumes. Whatever
`GROUP BY` returns is the answer the data gives. The gap between those two
numbers is what the rest of this sector is about.

## Hint 2

There is a second reason to avoid `BETWEEN` here that lesson 18 made and is
worth repeating: `created_at BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2023-10-31'` excludes
everything after midnight on the 31st, so it drops almost a whole day. The
half-open form `>= start AND < next_start` has no edge case, in any unit,
ever.

## Hint 3

Try the same query for product 1, then for all products at once. With all
ten thousand products the series is dense and the problem disappears — which
is exactly why this bug survives so long in production. It shows up on
filtered, segmented, low-volume slices: one customer, one region, one error
type. The dashboard that aggregates everything looks perfect.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex1 — the series as GROUP BY gives it: gappy.
SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
       count(*) AS reviews
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42
  AND created_at >= timestamptz '2023-10-01 00:00+00'
  AND created_at <  timestamptz '2023-11-01 00:00+00'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex1 — same series, bucket via date_trunc on UTC.
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
       count(*) AS reviews
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42
  AND created_at >= timestamptz '2023-10-01 00:00+00'
  AND created_at <  timestamptz '2023-11-01 00:00+00'
GROUP BY date_trunc('day', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')
ORDER BY 1;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the spine

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The same series as ex1, with every day of October
present and quiet days reading `0`.

Columns, in this order:

1. `day` — a `date`
2. `reviews`

**Ordered by `day` ascending. Exactly 31 rows**, whatever the data does.

Generate the calendar with `generate_series(date '2023-10-01', date
'2023-10-31', interval '1 day')`, put it on the **left** of the join, and
`coalesce` the count — not the day.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two independent things: the list of days you want, and the counts you have.
Build each separately, then attach the second to the first.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-10-01', date '2023-10-31',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
), daily AS (
    SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day, count(*) AS n
    FROM reviews WHERE product_id = 42 AND ... GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT s.day, coalesce(d.n, 0) AS reviews
FROM spine s LEFT JOIN daily d ON d.day = s.day
ORDER BY s.day;
```

## Hint 3

`generate_series` with `date` endpoints and an `interval` step returns
`timestamp`, so the `::date` cast is doing real work — without it your join
compares a `timestamp` to a `date`, which works but leaves a `timestamp` in
the output column. Decide whether the `daily` CTE still needs its own date
filter now that the spine bounds the result, and what each choice costs.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the failure before you make it. Write `daily d LEFT JOIN spine s`
instead and ask what comes back: every row of `daily`, plus a matching spine
day. That is the gappy series again, with an extra join. The direction is not
a detail; it is the entire technique.

## Hint 2

`coalesce` belongs on `d.n`. If you find yourself writing `coalesce(s.day,
d.day)` you have a join whose key can be NULL on the driving side, which
cannot happen with a generated spine — so that expression is evidence of a
mistake rather than a defence against one.

## Hint 3

About the `daily` CTE's own `WHERE`: it is redundant for correctness, because
the join drops anything outside October anyway. It is not redundant for
performance — without it, `daily` aggregates every review this product ever
received before throwing most of them away. Keeping the filter in both places
is the normal, correct choice, and being able to say why is the difference
between copying the idiom and understanding it.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex2 — spine on the left, coalesce on the measure.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-10-01', date '2023-10-31',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
), daily AS (
    SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
           count(*) AS n
    FROM reviews
    WHERE product_id = 42
      AND created_at >= timestamptz '2023-10-01 00:00+00'
      AND created_at <  timestamptz '2023-11-01 00:00+00'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT s.day,
       coalesce(d.n, 0) AS reviews
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN daily d ON d.day = s.day
ORDER BY s.day;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex2 — spine with a correlated count per day.
SELECT s.day,
       (SELECT count(*)
        FROM reviews r
        WHERE r.product_id = 42
          AND (r.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date = s.day) AS reviews
FROM (
    SELECT d::date AS day
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-10-01', date '2023-10-31',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
) s
ORDER BY s.day;

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — buckets `date_trunc` cannot make

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The clickstream team wants event volume in
six-hour blocks for 2023-10-20 UTC.

Columns, in this order:

1. `bucket` — the start of the six-hour block, a `timestamptz`
2. `events`

**Ordered by `bucket` ascending.** Four rows. Restrict to
`ts >= '2023-10-20 00:00+00'` and `< '2023-10-21 00:00+00'`.

`date_trunc` has no six-hour unit. `date_bin(stride, source, origin)` does:
give it `'6 hours'`, the column, and an explicit origin of
`timestamptz '2023-10-20 00:00+00'`. The origin is what makes the answer
reproducible — bins counted from an arbitrary instant are not the same bins
as bins counted from midnight.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Same grouped count as ex1, with a different expression producing the bucket.
Everything else is unchanged.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT date_bin(interval '6 hours', ts, timestamptz '2023-10-20 00:00+00')
           AS bucket,
       count(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE ts >= ... AND ts < ...
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

## Hint 3

`date_bin` refuses a stride containing months or years — `date_bin('1 month',
...)` raises an error, because a month is not a fixed duration and binning
needs one. That refusal is the function pointing you at `date_trunc`. Decide
what origin you would use if the business day started at 09:00 rather than
midnight, and notice that it is a one-token change.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The pre-14 way of doing this is worth writing once so you can recognise it:

```sql
to_timestamp(floor(extract(epoch FROM ts) / 21600) * 21600)
```

Divide the instant by the bucket width in seconds, floor, multiply back.
It works here — and only because 21600 divides a day evenly, so the implied
origin (1970-01-01 UTC) happens to align with midnight.

## Hint 2

Now break it in your head: change the stride to seven hours. The epoch
arithmetic silently produces buckets aligned to multiples of seven hours from
1970, which start at odd times of day and drift across dates. `date_bin` with
an explicit origin gives you the buckets you asked for. The lesson is not
"use the new function"; it is that the old idiom had a hidden parameter.

## Hint 3

`events.ts` is strictly increasing with `id` at one event per second, so each
six-hour bucket holds 21,600 rows and the four counts will be nearly
identical. That is a property of this dataset, not of clickstreams — but it
makes a useful check: if your four numbers are wildly unequal, your bucket
boundaries are not where you think they are.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex3 — fixed-width bins from an explicit origin.
SELECT date_bin(interval '6 hours', ts, timestamptz '2023-10-20 00:00+00') AS bucket,
       count(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE ts >= timestamptz '2023-10-20 00:00+00'
  AND ts <  timestamptz '2023-10-21 00:00+00'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex3 — the pre-14 epoch-arithmetic spelling.
SELECT to_timestamp(floor(extract(epoch FROM ts) / 21600) * 21600) AS bucket,
       count(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE ts >= timestamptz '2023-10-20 00:00+00'
  AND ts <  timestamptz '2023-10-21 00:00+00'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — whose day?

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The New York office wants event counts by **their**
calendar day, not by UTC.

Columns, in this order:

1. `day` — the `America/New_York` calendar day, as a `date`
2. `events`

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** Restrict the source rows to
`ts >= '2023-10-20 00:00+00'` and `< '2023-10-25 00:00+00'`.

In late October, New York is four hours behind UTC, so the first UTC hours of
each day belong to the previous New York day and the window's edges produce
partial days. Six rows come back, not five, and both edge rows are short —
that is correct, and it is exactly the kind of thing to explain on the chart
rather than in a follow-up email.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Convert the instant to the local wall clock first, then take the date of that
wall clock. Two operations, in that order.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT (ts AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')::date AS day, count(*) AS events
FROM events WHERE ... GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

## Hint 3

`ts AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'` applied to a `timestamptz` returns a
`timestamp` **without** time zone — the reading on a New York clock. Casting
that to `date` gives the local day. Applying `AT TIME ZONE` to a plain
`timestamp` does the opposite conversion, which is the single most confusing
thing in PostgreSQL's date handling; decide now which direction you are going
and write the type down in a comment.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a determinism question. `date_trunc('day', ts)` is not wrong —
it is *unspecified*, because it depends on the session's `TimeZone`. A report
whose answer changes with who runs it is not a report. Every expression in
this exercise names its zone explicitly, and that is the habit worth taking
away.

## Hint 2

Use `'America/New_York'`, never `'EST'`. The three-letter abbreviations are
fixed offsets with no knowledge of daylight saving, so `EST` is five hours
behind UTC in July — a time zone New York has never been in during summer.
The IANA names carry the full history of rule changes, which is why they are
the only safe choice.

## Hint 3

Predict the shape before you run it. New York is UTC-4 in late October, so
the New York day starts at 04:00 UTC. A window running from 2023-10-20 00:00
UTC therefore begins in the middle of New York's 19th, and ends in the middle
of its 24th — six local days touched, two of them partial. If you get five
rows, check whether your conversion ran in the wrong direction.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex4 — bucket by the local calendar day, named explicitly.
SELECT (ts AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')::date AS day,
       count(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE ts >= timestamptz '2023-10-20 00:00+00'
  AND ts <  timestamptz '2023-10-25 00:00+00'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex4 — the same local days via date_trunc.
SELECT date_trunc('day', ts AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')::date AS day,
       count(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE ts >= timestamptz '2023-10-20 00:00+00'
  AND ts <  timestamptz '2023-10-25 00:00+00'
GROUP BY date_trunc('day', ts AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')
ORDER BY 1;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — a calendar dimension

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Marketing believes weekends behave differently.
Build a calendar and prove or disprove it.

Generate every day from 2022-11-14 to 2023-11-14 inclusive with a weekend
flag (`extract(isodow FROM d) >= 6`), join the orders to it by UTC day, then
aggregate to months.

Columns, in this order:

1. `month` — the first day of the month, as a `date`
2. `days` — how many calendar days of that month are inside the range
3. `weekday_revenue` — `sum(total)` of non-cancelled orders on Mon–Fri
4. `weekend_revenue` — the same for Sat–Sun

**Ordered by `month` ascending.** Empty cells read `0`. Note that the first
and last months are partial, which is why `days` is in the output — a
revenue comparison without it invites a wrong conclusion.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three steps: a calendar CTE carrying the flag, a per-day revenue CTE, and a
join that aggregates both up to months. The calendar is the driving side, as
always.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH cal AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day,
           extract(isodow FROM d) >= 6 AS is_weekend
    FROM generate_series(date '2022-11-14', date '2023-11-14',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
), daily AS (
    SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT date_trunc('month', c.day)::date AS month, ...
FROM cal c LEFT JOIN daily d ON d.day = c.day
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

## Hint 3

`isodow` numbers Monday 1 through Sunday 7, so `>= 6` is the weekend.
`extract(dow ...)` numbers Sunday 0 through Saturday 6, so the same test
written with `dow` would be wrong in two different ways at once. The monthly
aggregation uses `count(*)` for `days` — the calendar guarantees one row per
day — and `sum(...) FILTER (WHERE is_weekend)` for the split. Decide where
your `coalesce` goes and why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice what putting the flag in the calendar buys. The definition of
"weekend" now appears exactly once, in a row the query produces, rather than
being an `extract` scattered through six expressions. When the Gulf office
says their weekend is Friday and Saturday, you change one line — and a real
date dimension makes that a column, not a predicate.

## Hint 2

Ask what `days` is protecting you against. November 2022 contributes 17 days
and November 2023 contributes 14, so their revenue is mechanically lower than
a full month's. Every partial-period report needs either the denominator or a
footnote; giving the reader `days` lets them compute a daily rate and reach
the right conclusion without you.

## Hint 3

If you want the honest version of marketing's question, divide: weekend
revenue per weekend day versus weekday revenue per weekday day. That needs
two more counts — `count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_weekend)` and its complement —
and turns a misleading comparison of totals into a comparable rate. Write it
as an extra column and see whether the belief survives.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex5 — a calendar dimension with a weekend flag.
WITH cal AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day,
           extract(isodow FROM d) >= 6 AS is_weekend
    FROM generate_series(date '2022-11-14', date '2023-11-14',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
), daily AS (
    SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
           sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT date_trunc('month', c.day)::date AS month,
       count(*) AS days,
       coalesce(sum(d.revenue) FILTER (WHERE NOT c.is_weekend), 0) AS weekday_revenue,
       coalesce(sum(d.revenue) FILTER (WHERE c.is_weekend), 0)     AS weekend_revenue
FROM cal c
LEFT JOIN daily d ON d.day = c.day
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex5 — flag computed per order, days counted separately.
WITH cal AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day
    FROM generate_series(date '2022-11-14', date '2023-11-14',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
), day_counts AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', day)::date AS month, count(*) AS days
    FROM cal GROUP BY 1
), rev AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', (o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'))::date AS month,
           sum(o.total) FILTER (
               WHERE extract(isodow FROM (o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')) < 6) AS weekday_revenue,
           sum(o.total) FILTER (
               WHERE extract(isodow FROM (o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')) >= 6) AS weekend_revenue
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
      AND (o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date
          BETWEEN date '2022-11-14' AND date '2023-11-14'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT dc.month,
       dc.days,
       coalesce(r.weekday_revenue, 0) AS weekday_revenue,
       coalesce(r.weekend_revenue, 0) AS weekend_revenue
FROM day_counts dc
LEFT JOIN rev r ON r.month = dc.month
ORDER BY dc.month;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a rolling average that means seven days

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Take the gap-filled October series from ex2 and add
a seven-day trailing average.

Columns, in this order:

1. `day`
2. `reviews`
3. `avg7` — the mean of `reviews` over this day and the six before it,
   rounded to 2 decimals

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** 31 rows.

Use a `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` frame. The
first six rows average fewer than seven days — that is correct, and whether
a dashboard should blank them is a product decision, not a SQL one.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The spine from ex2 becomes a CTE; the average is a window function over it,
ordered by day.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT day, reviews,
       round(avg(reviews) OVER (ORDER BY day
             RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2)
           AS avg7
FROM filled
ORDER BY day;
```

## Hint 3

An interval-offset `RANGE` frame requires exactly one `ORDER BY` column whose
type supports interval arithmetic — `date` qualifies. `avg` over `bigint`
returns `numeric`, so `round(x, 2)` works without a cast. Decide what you
would do if the requirement were "seven days centred on this one" and check
whether your frame syntax extends to it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run it with `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` as well and compare.
On this complete spine the two are identical, because there is exactly one
row per day. Now imagine removing the spine: `ROWS` would average the last
seven *observations*, which on product 42's real data might span three weeks,
while still being labelled a seven-day average. That is the bug the spine
prevents, and it is invisible in the output.

## Hint 2

There is a third frame mode, `GROUPS`, which counts distinct ordering values
rather than rows. It is the right tool when a series has several rows per
day and you want "seven days" without pre-aggregating. Knowing all three
exist — and that the default is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND
CURRENT ROW`, peers included — is what stops window frames feeling like
guesswork.

## Hint 3

Consider the edges honestly. A trailing average that starts on day one is
computed over one day and looks like a spike or a dip depending on the data.
Real dashboards either blank the first n-1 rows, or show them with a
different line style, or extend the spine backwards so the frame is always
full. Each is defensible; silently plotting a one-day "seven-day average" is
not.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex6 — a trailing average defined in days, not rows.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-10-01', date '2023-10-31',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
), daily AS (
    SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day, count(*) AS n
    FROM reviews
    WHERE product_id = 42
      AND created_at >= timestamptz '2023-10-01 00:00+00'
      AND created_at <  timestamptz '2023-11-01 00:00+00'
    GROUP BY 1
), filled AS (
    SELECT s.day, coalesce(d.n, 0) AS reviews
    FROM spine s LEFT JOIN daily d ON d.day = s.day
)
SELECT day,
       reviews,
       round(avg(reviews) OVER (ORDER BY day
             RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg7
FROM filled
ORDER BY day;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex6 — same window, ROWS frame over a complete spine.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-10-01', date '2023-10-31',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
), filled AS (
    SELECT s.day,
           (SELECT count(*)
            FROM reviews r
            WHERE r.product_id = 42
              AND (r.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date = s.day) AS reviews
    FROM spine s
)
SELECT day,
       reviews,
       round(avg(reviews) OVER (ORDER BY day
             ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg7
FROM filled
ORDER BY day;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — month over month, after the spine

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Five-star reviews for products 1, 2 and 3, monthly,
across the whole of 2023.

Columns, in this order:

1. `month` — the first of the month, as a `date`
2. `reviews` — five-star reviews for those three products that month
3. `prev_reviews` — the previous month's value, NULL for January
4. `pct_change` — `100 * (reviews - prev_reviews) / prev_reviews`, rounded
   to 1 decimal; NULL when `prev_reviews` is NULL or zero

**Ordered by `month` ascending. Twelve rows**, January to December 2023.

The population is deliberately thin, so some months may have none. Build the
spine first: `lag()` over an unfilled series returns *the previous row that
exists*, which is not the previous month, and a report labelled "MoM" that
compares March with January is worse than no report.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three stages: the twelve-month spine, the counts joined onto it with
`coalesce`, and the window function over the filled result.

## Hint 2

```sql
), filled AS (
    SELECT s.month, coalesce(m.n, 0) AS reviews
    FROM spine s LEFT JOIN monthly m ON m.month = s.month
)
SELECT month, reviews,
       lag(reviews) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_reviews,
       ...
FROM filled;
```

## Hint 3

Compute the lag once in a CTE and reuse it, or repeat the `lag(...) OVER
(...)` expression in the percentage — you cannot reference an output alias
from another select-list expression. For the division, `nullif(prev, 0)`
turns a zero denominator into NULL rather than an error. Decide whether a
month going from 0 to 5 should show NULL or "infinite growth", and be able to
defend the answer you ship.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Make the bug happen once, deliberately. Run the query without the spine and
look at the `prev_reviews` column: wherever a month is missing, the row after
it compares against two months back while still being labelled "previous".
Nothing in the output says so. That silence is why this is one of the most
common wrong numbers in business reporting.

## Hint 2

There is a related trap the spine does not fix: "the same month last year" is
not `lag(reviews, 12)` unless the series is complete *and* starts at a month
boundary that makes the offset land correctly. The robust spelling is a
self-join on `month = other.month + interval '1 year'`, which says what you
mean and cannot be knocked out of alignment.

## Hint 3

Percentage change has three edge cases and you should decide all three before
writing the expression: previous is NULL (no prior period — NULL), previous is
zero (undefined — NULL, not infinity, and not 100), and current is zero with a
non-zero previous (-100.0, which is a real and important number). A report
that silently produces a division error on the second case will be discovered
by a stakeholder, not by you.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex7 — spine first, then lag() means what it says.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS month
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-01-01', date '2023-12-01',
                         interval '1 month') AS d
), monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month,
           count(*) AS n
    FROM reviews
    WHERE product_id IN (1, 2, 3)
      AND rating = 5
      AND created_at >= timestamptz '2023-01-01 00:00+00'
      AND created_at <  timestamptz '2024-01-01 00:00+00'
    GROUP BY 1
), filled AS (
    SELECT s.month, coalesce(m.n, 0) AS reviews
    FROM spine s
    LEFT JOIN monthly m ON m.month = s.month
), lagged AS (
    SELECT month, reviews,
           lag(reviews) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_reviews
    FROM filled
)
SELECT month,
       reviews,
       prev_reviews,
       round(100.0 * (reviews - prev_reviews) / nullif(prev_reviews, 0), 1) AS pct_change
FROM lagged
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex7 — previous month by self-join instead of lag().
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS month
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-01-01', date '2023-12-01',
                         interval '1 month') AS d
), filled AS (
    SELECT s.month,
           (SELECT count(*)
            FROM reviews r
            WHERE r.product_id IN (1, 2, 3)
              AND r.rating = 5
              AND date_trunc('month', r.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date = s.month
           ) AS reviews
    FROM spine s
)
SELECT f.month,
       f.reviews,
       p.reviews AS prev_reviews,
       round(100.0 * (f.reviews - p.reviews) / nullif(p.reviews, 0), 1) AS pct_change
FROM filled f
LEFT JOIN filled p ON p.month = (f.month - interval '1 month')::date
ORDER BY f.month;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the week that changes year

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Weekly order counts across the 2022/2023 New Year,
labelled by ISO year and week.

Columns, in this order:

1. `iso_week` — text, formatted `IYYY-IW` (for example `2022-52`)
2. `orders`

**Ordered by `iso_week` ascending.** Orders with
`created_at >= '2022-12-26 00:00+00'` and `< '2023-01-09 00:00+00'`, bucketed
on the UTC calendar.

ISO weeks run Monday to Sunday and belong to the year containing their
Thursday, so 2023-01-01 — a Sunday — is in week 52 of ISO year **2022**. Use
`IYYY`, not `YYYY`: the second one mixes the calendar year with the ISO week
number and produces a label that is both wrong and mis-sorted, once a year,
every year.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `to_char` call produces the whole label. The grouping key and the output
column are the same expression.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT to_char(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', 'IYYY-IW') AS iso_week,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE ... GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

## Hint 3

Try it with `'YYYY-IW'` and diff the two results. The rows for 2023-01-01
change from `2022-52` to `2023-52`, which sorts to the end and appears on a
chart as a stray bar in the future. Then decide which of `to_char(...,
'IYYY-IW')` and `extract(isoyear) || '-' || extract(week)` you would rather
read in a code review.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the definition rather than the format string. ISO 8601 says a
week belongs to the year containing its Thursday. Work out by hand which ISO
year the week of Monday 2022-12-26 belongs to — its Thursday is 2022-12-29,
so 2022 — and which one the week of Monday 2023-01-02 belongs to. Now you can
check the query's output instead of trusting it.

## Hint 2

There is a spelling that cannot go wrong: group by `date_trunc('week', ...)`,
which returns the Monday, and derive the label from that same value. Both the
bucket and its name then come from one expression, so they cannot disagree.
When a label and a grouping key are computed separately, sooner or later
somebody edits one of them.

## Hint 3

`extract(week FROM d)` is the ISO week number and `extract(isoyear FROM d)`
is the ISO year — but `extract(year FROM d)` is the calendar year, and mixing
those two is the same bug in a different costume. If you build the label by
concatenation, remember `lpad(..., 2, '0')`, or week 5 sorts after week 40.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex8 — ISO year-week labels, IYYY not YYYY.
SELECT to_char(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', 'IYYY-IW') AS iso_week,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= timestamptz '2022-12-26 00:00+00'
  AND created_at <  timestamptz '2023-01-09 00:00+00'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / ex8 — same labels built from the truncated Monday.
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AS monday
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= timestamptz '2022-12-26 00:00+00'
      AND created_at <  timestamptz '2023-01-09 00:00+00'
)
SELECT extract(isoyear FROM monday)::int::text
           || '-' || lpad(extract(week FROM monday)::int::text, 2, '0') AS iso_week,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM weekly
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the monthly dashboard

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. One query, the whole panel: monthly revenue
from non-cancelled orders, a three-month trailing average, the previous
month, and the change.

Columns, in this order:

1. `month` — the first of the month, as a `date`
2. `revenue` — `sum(total)` of non-cancelled orders in that month, `0` if
   none
3. `avg3` — the average of `revenue` over this month and the two before it,
   rounded to 2 decimals, computed with an interval `RANGE` frame
4. `prev_revenue` — the previous month's `revenue`, NULL for the first row
5. `pct_change` — percentage change against `prev_revenue`, 1 decimal, NULL
   when there is no previous month or it is zero

**Ordered by `month` ascending.** The spine runs from 2022-11-01 to
2023-11-01 inclusive — **thirteen rows**.

Two honesty notes belong on the chart, and you should be able to state both:
the first and last months are partial, because the data starts 2022-11-14 and
ends 2023-11-14; and `avg3` on the first two rows averages fewer than three
months.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Assemble it from the pieces you already built: ex2's spine join, ex6's
`RANGE` frame, ex7's `lag` and `nullif`. Nothing here is new; the difficulty
is keeping four columns' worth of edge cases straight at once.

## Hint 2

```sql
), filled AS (
    SELECT s.month, coalesce(m.revenue, 0) AS revenue
    FROM spine s LEFT JOIN monthly m ON m.month = s.month
), win AS (
    SELECT month, revenue,
           round(avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                 RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '2 months' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg3,
           lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue
    FROM filled
)
```

## Hint 3

`RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '2 months' PRECEDING` is calendar-aware: from
2023-03-01 it reaches back to 2023-01-01 and includes January, February and
March. That is three months regardless of their differing lengths, which is
precisely what a `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING` frame would also give on a
complete spine — so decide which one you want to be reading in six months and
why, rather than picking the shorter one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build it in four commits, not one. Get `month` and `revenue` right and check
the thirteen rows. Add `avg3` and hand-check row three. Add `prev_revenue`
and confirm row one is NULL. Add `pct_change` last, because it is the column
with three separate NULL cases in it. Each step is checkable; the whole thing
in one go is not.

## Hint 2

Interrogate the partial months. November 2022 covers 14 days and November
2023 covers 14 days, so their revenue is roughly half a normal month's and
`pct_change` will show a dramatic-looking collapse on the last row. That
number is arithmetically correct and analytically worthless. The professional
move is to either clip the spine to complete months or carry a `days` column
so the reader can normalise — the same lesson ex5 made.

## Hint 3

Check the whole thing against an invariant: `sum(revenue)` across your
thirteen rows must equal `SELECT sum(total) FROM orders WHERE status <>
'cancelled'`. If it does not, either your spine does not cover the data or
your month bucketing disagrees with your filter — the two most likely
failures in a dashboard query, and the reason to check rather than admire.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / challenge — spine, gap fill, RANGE frame, lag.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS month
    FROM generate_series(date '2022-11-01', date '2023-11-01',
                         interval '1 month') AS d
), monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month,
           sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY 1
), filled AS (
    SELECT s.month, coalesce(m.revenue, 0) AS revenue
    FROM spine s
    LEFT JOIN monthly m ON m.month = s.month
), win AS (
    SELECT month,
           revenue,
           round(avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                 RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '2 months' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg3,
           lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue
    FROM filled
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       avg3,
       prev_revenue,
       round(100.0 * (revenue - prev_revenue) / nullif(prev_revenue, 0), 1) AS pct_change
FROM win
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / challenge — same panel with a ROWS frame and a self-join.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS month
    FROM generate_series(date '2022-11-01', date '2023-11-01',
                         interval '1 month') AS d
), filled AS (
    SELECT s.month,
           coalesce((SELECT sum(o.total)
                     FROM orders o
                     WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
                       AND date_trunc('month', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date
                           = s.month), 0) AS revenue
    FROM spine s
), win AS (
    SELECT month, revenue,
           round(avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                 ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg3
    FROM filled
)
SELECT w.month,
       w.revenue,
       w.avg3,
       p.revenue AS prev_revenue,
       round(100.0 * (w.revenue - p.revenue) / nullif(p.revenue, 0), 1) AS pct_change
FROM win w
LEFT JOIN filled p ON p.month = (w.month - interval '1 month')::date
ORDER BY w.month;

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — carry the last value forward

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. For every day of October 2023, the most recent
rating product 42 received **on or before that day**, carried forward across
the days with no reviews.

Columns, in this order:

1. `day` — a `date`, every day of October
2. `last_rating` — the rating of the latest October review on or before that
   day, or NULL for days before the product's first October review

**Ordered by `day` ascending. 31 rows.** Consider only reviews with
`created_at >= '2023-10-01 00:00+00'` and `< '2023-11-01 00:00+00'`. When a
day has several reviews, the latest one wins — break ties by `id` descending
so the answer is reproducible.

This is the other half of gap filling: sometimes the honest value for a quiet
period is not zero but "the same as last time".

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f04_time_buckets_calendars review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Spine first, as always. Then, for each day of the spine, the question is
"what is the latest review at or before the end of this day" — which is a
per-row lookup, not an aggregate.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT s.day, v.rating AS last_rating
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT r.rating
    FROM reviews r
    WHERE r.product_id = 42
      AND r.created_at >= timestamptz '2023-10-01 00:00+00'
      AND r.created_at <  (s.day + 1)::timestamptz
    ORDER BY r.created_at DESC, r.id DESC
    LIMIT 1
) v ON true
ORDER BY s.day;
```

## Hint 3

`LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` is the idiom for "attach this per-row
subquery, and keep the row even when it finds nothing" — a plain `CROSS JOIN
LATERAL` would drop the early days that have no prior review, which is
exactly the rows the prompt asks you to keep as NULL. Decide whether
`(s.day + 1)::timestamptz` is the right upper bound and what it assumes about
the session time zone.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is a one-pass alternative worth learning, and it is a genuinely
beautiful trick. Left-join the spine to each day's last rating, leaving NULLs
in the quiet days. Then:

```sql
count(rating) OVER (ORDER BY day)
```

counts the non-NULL values seen so far, which is constant across a run of
NULLs and increments at each real value — so it is an island id. Group by it
and every row in an island can take that island's single non-NULL value with
`max(rating) OVER (PARTITION BY grp)`.

## Hint 2

Compare the two approaches on cost. The `LATERAL` version does one indexed
lookup per spine row: 31 lookups here, 3,653 for a decade, each cheap but
each a separate probe. The window version reads the joined series once and
does two passes of window arithmetic. Below a few thousand rows neither
matters; above a million, only one of them is a good idea.

## Hint 3

Think about what NULL means at the start of the series. Days before the first
October review have no prior value *within the window you were told to
consider*, so they are NULL — but the product almost certainly had reviews in
September. Whether the report should reach back before its own window is a
requirements question, and the fact that the prompt pinned it means somebody
had to decide. Notice that; it is what separates a specification from a
request.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / review1 — last known value via a LATERAL lookup.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-10-01', date '2023-10-31',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
)
SELECT s.day,
       v.rating AS last_rating
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT r.rating
    FROM reviews r
    WHERE r.product_id = 42
      AND r.created_at >= timestamptz '2023-10-01 00:00+00'
      AND r.created_at <  ((s.day + 1)::timestamp AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')
    ORDER BY r.created_at DESC, r.id DESC
    LIMIT 1
) v ON true
ORDER BY s.day;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f04_time_buckets_calendars / review1 — forward fill by counting non-nulls into islands.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT d::date AS day
    FROM generate_series(date '2023-10-01', date '2023-10-31',
                         interval '1 day') AS d
), day_last AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON ((created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date)
           (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
           rating
    FROM reviews
    WHERE product_id = 42
      AND created_at >= timestamptz '2023-10-01 00:00+00'
      AND created_at <  timestamptz '2023-11-01 00:00+00'
    ORDER BY (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date, created_at DESC, id DESC
), joined AS (
    SELECT s.day, dl.rating
    FROM spine s
    LEFT JOIN day_last dl ON dl.day = s.day
), islands AS (
    SELECT day, rating,
           count(rating) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS grp
    FROM joined
)
SELECT day,
       max(rating) OVER (PARTITION BY grp) AS last_rating
FROM islands
ORDER BY day;

lessons.title: V3·F5 — Cohort and retention analysis
lessons.summary: A cohort is a population pinned to the moment it entered, and retention is what fraction of it comes back in each period since. The SQL is a grid; the difficulty is the denominator, the period index, and knowing which cells of the triangle you are not allowed to look at yet.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·F5 — Cohort and retention analysis

Every metric that averages over "all customers" is contaminated. Growth adds
new users faster than old ones churn, so the average looks like it is
improving while every individual month gets worse — and it looks like it is
collapsing during a hiring freeze while the product is fine. The fix is to
stop averaging across entry dates: pin each customer to the period they
arrived in, and measure that group on its own timeline.

That is a cohort. The output is a triangle: rows are cohorts, columns are
periods since entry, cells are the fraction still active. The SQL that builds
it is not hard. The three things that are hard are the denominator, the
period index, and knowing which cells you are not entitled to look at.

## Concept

Three steps, always in this order.

**1. Assign each subject to a cohort.**

```sql
SELECT id,
       date_trunc('month', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS cohort_month
FROM customers;
```

The cohort key is a property of the *subject*, fixed forever. Signup month is
the usual choice; first-purchase month is the other common one, and they
answer different questions — the first measures the funnel from acquisition,
the second measures the product for people who actually used it.

**2. Turn activity into (cohort, period) pairs.**

```sql
(extract(year FROM order_month) * 12 + extract(month FROM order_month))
  - (extract(year FROM cohort_month) * 12 + extract(month FROM cohort_month))
    AS period
```

Period 0 is the cohort's own month. Subtracting month boundaries this way is
exact; subtracting dates and dividing by 30 is not, and the drift shows up as
a diagonal smear in the triangle.

**3. Divide by the cohort's size, not by the period's population.**

```sql
round(100.0 * count(DISTINCT customer_id) / cohort_size, 1)
```

The denominator is how many customers entered in that cohort — every period,
unchanged. Dividing by "customers active this month" produces a number that
cannot go down and means nothing.

**The triangle is right-censored.** Data ends on a date. A cohort three
months old has no period-6 cell, and the correct value there is NULL, not
zero. Reports that fill the missing corner with zeros show every recent
cohort collapsing, and somebody always believes it.

**And left-truncated, here.** Signups span 2021-11-14 to 2023-11-14; orders
only 2022-11-14 to 2023-11-14. A customer who signed up in 2022-01 and bought
in 2022-03 has an invisible period 2. Every cohort before 2022-11 is missing
its early periods entirely, and no query can recover them.

**Count people, not events.** `count(DISTINCT customer_id)` is not a
performance footnote here; it is the definition. A customer who placed four
orders in March is one retained customer, and `count(*)` over the joined
rows produces retention above 100% — the fan-out bug from the first sector,
wearing an analytics hat. On large event tables the cheap spelling is to
reduce to one row per (customer, period) with a single `SELECT DISTINCT`
first, then count plainly.

**Two cohort definitions, two questions.** Signup cohorts include everyone
who arrived, so period 0 is the activation rate and the whole curve moves
when marketing changes. First-purchase cohorts condition on activation, so
period 0 is 100% by construction and the curve measures the product for the
people who actually used it. Both are legitimate; putting them on one chart
without saying which is which is how two teams end up defending different
numbers for the same metric.

## Exercise 1 — the cohorts themselves

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Signup cohorts by month. Columns: `cohort_month`,
`customers`. Ordered by `cohort_month`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex1`

## Exercise 2 — activation

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Per cohort: size, how many ever placed a
non-cancelled order, and the rate. Columns: `cohort_month`, `customers`,
`buyers`, `pct_activated`. Ordered by `cohort_month`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex2`

## Exercise 3 — the long form

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. One row per (cohort month, activity month) for 2023
signup cohorts. Columns: `cohort_month`, `order_month`, `buyers`. Ordered by
both.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the period index

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The same grid with `period` — whole months since
the cohort month — instead of a calendar month. Columns: `cohort_month`,
`period`, `buyers`. Ordered by both.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex4`

## Exercise 5 — the denominator

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Add the cohort size and the retention rate.
Columns: `cohort_month`, `cohort_size`, `period`, `buyers`, `pct`. Ordered
by `cohort_month`, `period`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex5`

## Exercise 6 — the triangle

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Pivot periods 0 to 5 into columns. Columns:
`cohort_month`, `cohort_size`, `m0` … `m5` as percentages. Ordered by
`cohort_month`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex6`

## Exercise 7 — repeat purchase from the first order

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Cohort by **first order month** and measure the
second purchase within 30, 60 and 90 days. Columns: `cohort_month`,
`buyers`, `d30`, `d60`, `d90`. Ordered by `cohort_month`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex7`

## Exercise 8 — where the active customers came from

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Decompose each month's active buyers into `new`,
`retained` and `resurrected`, plus the `churned` count from the month
before. Columns: `month`, `active`, `new`, `retained`, `resurrected`,
`churned`. Ordered by `month`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex8`

## Challenge — the honest triangle

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The `m0`–`m3` triangle again, but with NULL
in every cell the data cannot yet observe. Columns: `cohort_month`,
`cohort_size`, `m0`, `m1`, `m2`, `m3`. Ordered by `cohort_month`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: activation by market. Columns: `country`, `customers`,
`buyers`, `pct_activated`. Ordered by `country`.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3f05_cohorts_retention

A cohort analysis is three joins and a division. Every mistake in it is in
the division.

## Notes

**The cohort key belongs to the subject and never changes.** It is computed
once, from the customer's own row, and carried into every activity fact. If
you find yourself recomputing the cohort from the activity, you have built
something else — usually a monthly report with cohort-shaped column names.

**Period arithmetic must be exact.** `(y*12 + m)` for both months, then
subtract. Date differences divided by 30 drift by a day every other month
and by two days across a leap year, so activity slides between period
columns and the triangle develops a smear that looks like a real effect.
For day-based periods — 7-day, 30-day retention — subtract the timestamps
directly and floor; do not mix the two schemes in one report.

**The denominator is the cohort size.** Every period divides by the same
number: how many subjects entered. Two wrong denominators are common. Using
"customers active in that period" gives you a ratio of a set to itself.
Using "customers still active as of the previous period" gives you a
conditional survival rate, which is a legitimate metric and a completely
different one — say which you mean in the column name.

**`count(DISTINCT customer_id)`, not `count(*)`.** A customer who placed four
orders in a month is one retained customer. This is the fan-out bug from the
first sector wearing an analytics hat, and it inflates retention above 100%
in a way that is embarrassing rather than subtle.

**Right censoring is not zero.** A cohort that is two months old has no
period-5 observation. NULL is the truthful value; zero is a claim that
nobody came back. Fill the corner with zeros and every chart shows recent
cohorts falling off a cliff — the single most common false alarm in
retention reporting.

**Left truncation is this dataset's version of the same disease.** Orders
begin 2022-11-14, so cohorts from 2021 and most of 2022 have unobservable
early periods. Their period-0 cell is not "these customers did not buy"; it
is "we were not looking". A report that does not exclude or flag those rows
is misleading regardless of how correct the SQL is.

**Retention shape matters more than any single number.** A curve that drops
steeply then flattens has a loyal core; one that decays smoothly has none. A
period-1 number in isolation tells you nothing, which is why the triangle is
the deliverable and the headline figure is the summary.

**Signup cohorts and first-purchase cohorts answer different questions.**
Signup cohorts include people who never activated, so the whole curve sits
lower and moves when marketing changes. First-purchase cohorts condition on
activation and measure the product. Neither is more correct; mixing them in
one dashboard is.

## ex1 — the cohorts themselves

What this tested: that a cohort is a bucketed property of the subject, not
of the activity. The classic mistake is to bucket by first order date and
call it a signup cohort — a different population entirely, since it silently
drops everyone who never ordered.

## ex2 — activation

What this tested: an anti-join-flavoured rate with an honest denominator.
Every customer is in the denominator, including the ones who never appear in
`orders` — which is why the count must come from `customers` and not from
the join. The classic mistake is an inner join, which quietly makes the rate
100%.

## ex3 — the long form

What this tested: producing (cohort, activity period) pairs at the right
grain. `count(DISTINCT customer_id)` is the whole exercise: without it you
are counting orders and calling them people. The classic mistake is grouping
by `customer_id` somewhere in the middle and losing the ability to count
distinct customers at all.

## ex4 — the period index

What this tested: exact month arithmetic. `age()` and date subtraction both
tempt you here and both are wrong in ways that only show up months later.
The classic mistake is `(order_month - cohort_month) / 30`, which is
approximately right and therefore hard to find.

## ex5 — the denominator

What this tested: joining a per-cohort scalar onto per-period rows without
changing the grain. Aggregate the sizes separately and join, or carry them
with a window — both work; recomputing the size inside the grouped query does
not, because the group is a (cohort, period) pair.

## ex6 — the triangle

What this tested: the pivot from the previous sector applied to a period
index. Because the spread key is `period`, and periods are integers, the
column list is finite and writable. The classic mistake is `coalesce(..., 0)`
on cells that are censored rather than empty — which the challenge makes you
undo.

## ex7 — repeat purchase from the first order

What this tested: day-based windows and a self-referential population. Each
customer's clock starts at their own first order, so the comparison is
per-customer, not per-calendar-month. The classic mistake is counting the
first order itself as the repeat — the second purchase must be strictly
later, and `>` versus `>=` is the whole difference.

## ex8 — where the active customers came from

What this tested: classification rather than counting. Each active customer
in a month is exactly one of new, retained or resurrected, so those three
must sum to `active` — a strong invariant worth asserting. `churned` belongs
to the previous month's population and is therefore not part of that sum,
which is the subtlety that makes this decomposition worth writing once by
hand.

## challenge — the honest triangle

What this tested: knowing what you are not allowed to know. A cell is
observable only if the cohort's period-n month has fully elapsed within the
data. Encoding that as a `CASE` on the month index — rather than trusting the
absence of rows — is the difference between a report that is silent about its
limits and one that states them.

## review1 — activation by market

Same rate, different cut. The point is that the cohort dimension does not
have to be time: any stable property of the subject at entry — country, plan,
channel, campaign — forms cohorts, and the same denominator discipline
applies. Countries with few customers will have noisy rates, which is an
argument for showing the denominator next to every rate you publish.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — `count(DISTINCT ...)`, `count(*) FILTER`, and what each costs.
- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc`, `extract(year/month)`, `age()` and interval arithmetic.
- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — carrying a per-partition total onto every row without a second aggregate.
- [`SELECT` — `DISTINCT ON`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the compact way to get each customer's first order.
- [`GROUPING SETS`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — margins on a cohort table when someone asks for an "all cohorts" row.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·F5 — Cohort and retention analysis

The archive version: the three steps, the denominators, the censoring, and
the arguments.

## 1. What a cohort is

A cohort is a set of subjects grouped by **when they entered**, measured on a
clock that starts at entry. The point is to remove the confound that makes
aggregate metrics uninterpretable: in a growing business, "average retention
across all customers" is dominated by whoever joined most recently, so it
moves when acquisition moves and says nothing about the product.

Three ingredients:

| ingredient | example | notes |
|---|---|---|
| entry event | signup, first order, activation | fixed per subject, forever |
| activity event | order, login, session | many per subject |
| period index | months since entry | integer, starts at 0 |

## 2. The canonical query

```sql
WITH cohort AS (
    SELECT id AS customer_id,
           date_trunc('month', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS cohort_month
    FROM customers
), sizes AS (
    SELECT cohort_month, count(*) AS cohort_size
    FROM cohort GROUP BY 1
), activity AS (
    SELECT c.cohort_month,
           c.customer_id,
           date_trunc('month', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS order_month
    FROM orders o
    JOIN cohort c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
), grid AS (
    SELECT cohort_month,
           (extract(year FROM order_month) * 12 + extract(month FROM order_month))
             - (extract(year FROM cohort_month) * 12 + extract(month FROM cohort_month))
               AS period,
           count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS buyers
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT g.cohort_month, s.cohort_size, g.period, g.buyers,
       round(100.0 * g.buyers / s.cohort_size, 1) AS pct
FROM grid g JOIN sizes s USING (cohort_month)
ORDER BY g.cohort_month, g.period;
```

Read it as: label the subjects, count the labels, label the activity, count
per (label, period), divide by the label count.

## 3. Period arithmetic

```sql
-- months between two month boundaries: exact
(extract(year FROM b) * 12 + extract(month FROM b))
  - (extract(year FROM a) * 12 + extract(month FROM a))

-- whole days between two instants: exact
floor(extract(epoch FROM (b - a)) / 86400)::int

-- weeks since entry
floor(extract(epoch FROM (b - a)) / (86400 * 7))::int

-- WRONG: drifts
(b::date - a::date) / 30
```

Pick one scheme per report. A "monthly" triangle whose columns are really
30-day windows is a different analysis with the same axis labels, and the two
diverge by a whole column after a year.

## 4. Denominators, three of them

```sql
-- classic retention: share of the cohort active in period n
buyers_n / cohort_size

-- conditional survival: share of period n-1's survivors still here
buyers_n / buyers_(n-1)

-- unbounded / "ever again": share of the cohort active in period n or later
```

They answer "how much of the cohort is left", "what is this period's churn
rate", and "how many are not gone forever". All three are legitimate; only
the first is what "retention" means without qualification. Name the column
after the one you computed.

## 5. Censoring and truncation

**Right censoring**: for a cohort entering at month *c*, period *n* is
observable only if month *c+n* has completely elapsed inside the data. Encode
it:

```sql
CASE WHEN cohort_month + (n || ' months')::interval
          <= date '2023-11-01' THEN pct END AS m3
```

**Left truncation**: activity data starts later than subject data. On this
dataset, orders begin 2022-11-14 while signups begin 2021-11-14, so every
cohort before 2022-11 is missing its early periods. Those cells are not zero
and are not merely censored — they are unobservable, permanently. Either
restrict the cohorts to those whose period 0 falls inside the activity
window, or flag them.

**Partial periods** are the third one. If the data ends on the 14th, the
final month is half a month, so its activity is mechanically low. Exclude it
or show the elapsed fraction.

## 6. Two cohort definitions

```sql
-- signup cohort: includes never-buyers, moves with marketing
date_trunc('month', c.created_at)

-- first-purchase cohort: conditions on activation, measures the product
SELECT customer_id, date_trunc('month', min(created_at)) AS cohort_month
FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY customer_id
```

A signup cohort's period-0 retention is the activation rate. A first-purchase
cohort's period-0 retention is 100% by construction — which is a useful sanity
check and a useless chart column.

## 7. Active-user decomposition

The other standard view, and a good exercise in classification:

```
active(m)      = new(m) + retained(m) + resurrected(m)
new(m)         = first-ever activity is in m
retained(m)    = active in m and in m-1
resurrected(m) = active in m, not in m-1, but active at some point before
churned(m)     = active in m-1, not in m           -- belongs to m-1's population
```

The first line is an invariant: assert it. If the three parts do not sum to
`active`, a customer has been classified twice or not at all.

One more view worth having: **cumulative or "ever again" retention**, the
share of a cohort active in period *n* **or any later period**. Classic
retention is noisy because a customer who orders every seven weeks appears in
alternate months and looks like they churned and resurrected. The cumulative
version smooths that away and answers "how many are not gone for good", at
the cost of being monotonically non-increasing by construction and therefore
looking flatter than reality. Compute it by replacing the period equality
with `period >= n` in the filter, and label the column so nobody compares it
with the classic number.

## 8. Common mistakes

- `count(*)` instead of `count(DISTINCT customer_id)`.
- Dividing by the period's active population instead of the cohort size.
- Computing the cohort from activity and calling it a signup cohort.
- `coalesce(pct, 0)` over censored cells.
- Day arithmetic with `/ 30`.
- An inner join to `customers`, which drops the never-active subjects that
  belong in the denominator.
- Mixing signup cohorts and first-purchase cohorts on one chart.
- Ignoring the partial final period.
- Publishing a rate without its denominator, so nobody can see it came from
  eleven people.

## 9. The interview answer

> *"Walk me through a retention query."*

"Three steps. First I label every subject with their cohort — usually the
month they signed up, computed from the customer row so it never changes.
Second I join their activity and compute a period index as an exact month
difference, `(y*12+m)` on both sides and subtract, because dividing days by
30 drifts. Third I count distinct customers per (cohort, period) and divide
by the cohort's own size, which I compute separately so the denominator
doesn't move with the numerator. Then the two things people get wrong: the
cells the data can't observe yet must be NULL rather than zero, otherwise
every recent cohort looks like it collapsed; and if your activity table
starts later than your subject table, early cohorts are missing periods
permanently and should be excluded, not shown as zeros."

## Check yourself

1. Why is "average retention across all users" uninterpretable in a growing
   business?
2. Where does the cohort key come from, and why must it never be recomputed
   from activity?
3. Write exact month-difference arithmetic and say what breaks with `/ 30`.
4. Name three possible denominators and the question each answers.
5. Why `count(DISTINCT customer_id)`, and what does `count(*)` produce
   instead?
6. What is the correct value of an unobservable cell, and what goes wrong
   with zero?
7. Distinguish right censoring, left truncation and a partial final period.
8. What is period-0 retention for a first-purchase cohort, and why?
9. What does a signup cohort's period-0 number measure?
10. State the active-user decomposition invariant and how you would assert
    it.
11. A cohort of 9 customers shows 33.3% retention. What do you publish next
    to it?
12. Your triangle has a diagonal smear that moves one column every few
    months. What is the bug?
13. When would you deliberately use conditional survival instead of classic
    retention?
lessons.fullReading:
# The long read — the clock that starts when you arrive

## Where cohorts came from

Cohort analysis is not a growth-team invention; it is demography. A birth
cohort — everyone born in 1946 — is followed through life and measured on
age, not on calendar year, because comparing a 20-year-old in 1966 with a
20-year-old in 2006 is more informative than comparing 1966 with 2006. The
same logic reached epidemiology (survival analysis, Kaplan–Meier curves),
then actuarial work, then finally software.

The insight that transfers is that **calendar time and subject time are
different axes**, and aggregate metrics collapse them. A dashboard showing
"monthly active users" over calendar time mixes people on their first day
with people on their thousandth. When the number moves, you cannot tell
whether behaviour changed or the mix did. Cohorts separate the two, at the
cost of a report that is a triangle rather than a line — which is precisely
why executives dislike them and analysts insist on them.

The survival-analysis lineage also gives you the vocabulary for the hard
part. **Censoring** means a subject's outcome is not yet observed:
right-censored subjects are still under observation and have simply not
reached period *n* yet. **Truncation** means the subject was not observed at
all during some interval — the data collection started late, so early
periods do not exist. Retention dashboards routinely confuse the two and
paper over both with zeros, which is the analytical equivalent of reporting
that everyone who has not yet died is immortal.

## The shape of the query, and why it is always the same

Every cohort query in every dialect has the same skeleton because the data
model does: a subject table with one row per subject, an activity table with
many rows per subject, and a need to divide the second by a count taken from
the first.

The subtlety is grain. `cohort_size` is one number per cohort;
`buyers` is one number per (cohort, period). Combining them requires either
a join between two aggregates at different grains, or a window function that
carries the coarse number onto the fine rows:

```sql
sum(count(DISTINCT customer_id)) OVER (PARTITION BY cohort_month)
```

— which is *not* the cohort size, because it counts distinct customers per
period and then adds those up, double-counting anyone active in two periods.
That trap is worth staring at: the window version of the denominator is
wrong in a way that produces plausible numbers slightly under 100%. The
correct carry is a window over the cohort's *size*, computed from the subject
table, or a plain join. When in doubt, join.

## `count(DISTINCT)` and what it costs

`count(DISTINCT customer_id)` cannot share a sorted pass with other
aggregates: PostgreSQL sorts or hashes the column per group, per distinct
aggregate. A cohort grid with two or three `DISTINCT` counts over millions of
activity rows is genuinely expensive, and it does not parallelise as well as
plain aggregates.

The standard cure is to pre-reduce to one row per (customer, period) before
counting:

```sql
WITH monthly_active AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, cohort_month, period FROM activity
)
SELECT cohort_month, period, count(*) FROM monthly_active GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

One `DISTINCT` over three columns, then plain counts. On large event tables
this is not a micro-optimisation; it is the difference between a query that
finishes and one that does not. The same trick, at a different scale, is what
`HyperLogLog` extensions buy you when even the distinct pass is too much —
the last sector of this pack takes that up.

## The triangle, and reading it

The output is conventionally laid out with cohorts down the left and periods
across the top, producing a lower-left triangle: older cohorts have more
columns filled. Three readings, and a good analyst does all three:

- **Along a row** — one cohort's decay curve. Steep-then-flat is a product
  with a loyal core. Smoothly decaying is a product people churn out of at a
  constant hazard, which is much worse and much less obvious from a single
  number.
- **Down a column** — the same period across cohorts. This is the
  product-improvement view: is month-1 retention better for people who joined
  in June than for those who joined in January?
- **Along a diagonal** — everyone experiencing the same calendar month. A
  bad diagonal is an outage, a pricing change, or a holiday, not a cohort
  effect. Diagonals are how you catch things that have nothing to do with
  cohorts at all.

If a report only lets you read rows, it is a chart, not an analysis.

## Definitions people argue about

**What counts as active?** Any order? A non-cancelled order? A paid one? A
login? Each definition produces a different curve and all of them are called
"retention". Write it in the title.

**Which cohort key?** Signup date includes people who never activated and
therefore measures marketing as much as product; first-purchase date
conditions on activation and measures the product for people who used it.
Both are right. Publishing both without labelling them is how two teams end
up with different numbers and a meeting.

**Monthly or rolling?** Calendar-month retention asks "did they order in
March", which penalises someone who orders every 35 days. A 30-day rolling
window asks "did they order within 30 days of the period start", which is
kinder and harder to compute. Subscription businesses use calendar periods
because billing does; usage products usually should not.

**Does period 0 belong on the chart?** For a first-purchase cohort it is
100% by definition. For a signup cohort it is the activation rate, which is
a genuinely interesting number that has no business sharing an axis with
retention.

## Performance notes

- **Pre-reduce before counting distinct.** One `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id,
  cohort, period` then plain `count(*)` beats several `count(DISTINCT)`s.
- **Bucket once.** `date_trunc` on three million activity rows in three
  different places is three times the work; compute it in one CTE.
- **Join sizes late and small.** The cohort-size table has one row per
  cohort — tens of rows. Join it after the grid is aggregated, never before.
- **Index the activity's subject key.** The join from activity to cohort is
  the whole cost; without an index on `orders.customer_id` it is a hash join
  over the entire table every time. (This dataset deliberately lacks that
  index, which is a lesson from Part 5 you can feel here.)
- **Materialise the triangle.** Retention over a fixed history does not
  change. A nightly materialized view of (cohort, period, buyers) makes every
  downstream question instant.

## When not to use cohorts

- **When the population is tiny.** A cohort of eleven customers produces
  retention values of 9.1%, 18.2%, 27.3% and nothing in between. Publishing
  a percentage from a denominator under a few hundred invites confident
  conclusions about noise.
- **When there is no meaningful repeat.** Retention on a product people buy
  once — a mattress, a house survey — measures nothing. The right analysis is
  referral or lifetime value.
- **When the entry event is not well defined.** If "signup" happens twice for
  some users, or is backfilled, or means different things across two
  acquisition channels, the cohort key is unstable and everything downstream
  inherits that.
- **When the question is really about a single change.** "Did the March
  redesign help?" is a before/after comparison on the diagonal, and a cohort
  triangle is an expensive way to answer it badly.
- **When the answer will be a single headline number.** The value of the
  triangle is its shape. If the audience will only ever look at one cell,
  compute that cell and defend it, rather than shipping a grid nobody reads.

## The habit worth building

Before you write the query, write the denominator on paper and say the
sentence it makes: "of the *N* customers who signed up in March, *X* placed a
non-cancelled order in their third month". If that sentence is not true of
your SQL — if *N* moves between periods, or *X* counts orders instead of
people, or the third month has not happened yet — the query is wrong no
matter what it returns. Every retention bug is a sentence that does not hold
up when read aloud.

2. `customers` — how many signed up that month

**Ordered by `cohort_month` ascending.**

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is an ordinary monthly `GROUP BY` over `customers`. The only thing that
makes it a cohort is what you are going to do with it next.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS cohort_month,
       count(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

## Hint 3

No spine is needed here: signups are dense enough that every month in the
range has customers, and `customers` is the subject table, so a missing month
would mean nobody joined — which is information, not a gap to be filled.
Decide whether you would still add a spine if this were a report someone ran
weekly, and what would change.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice what is *not* in this query: `orders`. The cohort is a property of the
customer, computed from the customer's own row, and it exists whether or not
they ever bought anything. Every later exercise depends on that — the
denominator has to include the people who never showed up again, and it can
only do so if it was never joined to activity.

## Hint 2

Sanity-check the shape against what you know: signups run from 2021-11-14 to
2023-11-14, which touches 25 distinct months, and the first and last of them
cover roughly half a month each. If your first and last rows are not
noticeably smaller than the others, check your bucketing.

## Hint 3

The alternative cohort definition — month of first order — produces a
different and smaller population, because roughly five thousand customers
never ordered at all. Write that version too, count its rows, and keep both
in mind: ex7 uses it deliberately, and the difference between the two is the
activation rate ex2 computes.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f05_cohorts_retention / ex1 — cohorts are a property of the subject.
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS cohort_month,
       count(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:

WITH labelled AS (
    SELECT id,
           ((created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date
            - (extract(day FROM (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'))::int - 1)) AS cohort_month
    FROM customers
)

FROM labelled

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — activation

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. What fraction of each signup cohort ever became a
customer in the sense that matters — placed at least one non-cancelled
order?

Columns, in this order:

1. `cohort_month`
2. `customers` — the cohort's size
3. `buyers` — how many of them placed at least one order with
   `status <> 'cancelled'`
4. `pct_activated` — `buyers` as a percentage of `customers`, 1 decimal

**Ordered by `cohort_month` ascending.**

The denominator must be every customer in the cohort, including the ones who
never appear in `orders` at all — around five thousand customers across the
whole table have no orders. That means the count comes from `customers`, and
the join to `orders` must not be allowed to remove rows.

Read the numbers when they come back, and notice that the early cohorts are
not comparable to the late ones: order data begins 2022-11-14, so a customer
who signed up in 2022-01 and bought in 2022-03 looks like a non-buyer.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f05_cohorts_retention ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two numbers over the same population: how many customers, and how many of
them satisfy a condition. The condition is an existence test against
`orders`.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT date_trunc('month', c.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS cohort_month,
       count(*) AS customers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM orders o
           WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'cancelled')) AS buyers,
       ...
FROM customers c
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

## Hint 3

`count(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (...))` keeps both numbers in one pass over
`customers`, so the denominator cannot drift from the numerator. The
alternative — a `LEFT JOIN` to a per-customer aggregate, then
`count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.n IS NOT NULL)` — is equally correct. Decide which
you would rather read, then remember `100.0` in the percentage.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the wrong version deliberately and look at it:

```sql
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
```

Now `count(DISTINCT c.id)` is buyers *and* the denominator, so the activation
rate is 100% in every cohort. The bug is not the arithmetic; it is that the
join silently redefined the population. Every rate bug looks like this.

## Hint 2

Think about what this column means at the top and bottom of the table. The
2021 cohorts show a low activation rate not because those customers were bad
but because most of their buying happened before `orders` starts. That is
left truncation, and it is not fixable by any query — only by excluding or
flagging those cohorts. Decide how you would label the chart.

## Hint 3

`EXISTS` stops at the first matching row, which makes it cheaper than
`count(*) > 0` and much cheaper than joining and de-duplicating. On this
dataset `orders.customer_id` has no index, so the semi-join is a hash join
over half a million rows either way — but the habit of reaching for `EXISTS`
when the question is "any" rather than "how many" is worth having before it
matters.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f05_cohorts_retention / ex2 — the denominator is every customer, buyers or not.
SELECT date_trunc('month', c.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS cohort_month,
       count(*) AS customers,
       count(*) FILTER (
           WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                         WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
                           AND o.status <> 'cancelled')) AS buyers,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (
           WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                         WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
                           AND o.status <> 'cancelled')) / count(*), 1) AS pct_activated
FROM customers c
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f05_cohorts_retention / ex2 — buyers found by a LEFT JOIN to a per-customer set.
WITH buyers AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
    FROM orders
    WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
), labelled AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', c.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS cohort_month,
           (b.customer_id IS NOT NULL) AS activated
    FROM customers c
    LEFT JOIN buyers b ON b.customer_id = c.id
)
SELECT cohort_month,
       count(*) AS customers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE activated) AS buyers,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE activated) / count(*), 1) AS pct_activated
FROM labelled
GROUP BY cohort_month
ORDER BY cohort_month;

## Exercise 3 — the long form

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The cohort grid, before it becomes a triangle: one
row per (signup month, activity month) pair.

Restrict to customers who signed up in **2023** — those are the cohorts whose
whole life is inside the order data.

Columns, in this order:

1. `cohort_month` — the customer's signup month
2. `order_month` — the month of the activity
3. `buyers` — how many **distinct customers** of that cohort placed a
   non-cancelled order in that month

**Ordered by `cohort_month` ascending, then `order_month` ascending.**

`count(DISTINCT customer_id)`, not `count(*)`. A customer with four orders in
March is one retained customer, and counting rows instead of people is the
