# Reading - v3f08_sampling_approximation

Approximation is not sloppiness; it is choosing the precision the decision
needs and being able to say what the error is.

## Notes

**`count(*)` is a scan, and that is MVCC's fault, not PostgreSQL's
laziness.** Row visibility depends on the reading transaction's snapshot, so
there is no single true row count to cache. An index-only scan can help when
the visibility map is current, but there is no O(1) count. Every "why is
`count(*)` slow" question has this answer.

**`BERNOULLI` is statistically clean and reads everything.** It applies an
independent coin flip per row, so the sample is unbiased with respect to
anything. It still touches every page, so it saves the cost of the aggregate,
the join and the sort — not the I/O.

**`SYSTEM` skips I/O and buys clustering bias.** It selects pages and takes
all rows in them. When physical order correlates with your measure, the
sample is not random: `events.ts` is strictly increasing with `id` here, so a
`SYSTEM` sample of `events` is a sample of a handful of time windows. For
`orders`, whose values were generated independently of insertion order, it is
much better behaved — but "much better behaved on this dataset" is not a
property you can rely on in general.

**`REPEATABLE` is not optional for anything that gets read twice.** Without
it, running the report again gives different numbers, and nobody can tell
whether the business changed or the sample did.

**Hash sampling samples entities.** Two `TABLESAMPLE` calls are independent,
so joining two samples produces almost nothing — a 1% × 1% join is 0.01% of
the pairs. Hashing a shared key gives you a consistent slice of the *world*:
the same customers in every table, all their orders, all their events. It is
also stable over time, which means yesterday's sampled cohort is still
sampled today.

**Catalog estimates are free and stale.** `reltuples` and `relpages` come
from the last `ANALYZE` or `VACUUM`. On a table with heavy churn they can be
badly wrong; on an append-only table they lag by whatever the autovacuum
settings allow. Read `pg_stat_user_tables.last_analyze` before trusting them.

**`n_distinct` is signed, and the sign is the interesting part.** A positive
value is an absolute estimate. A negative value is a *ratio*: -0.5 means
"distinct values are half the row count", which is how the planner expresses
a cardinality that grows with the table. Multiply by `reltuples` to get an
absolute number. And treat it with suspicion: `n_distinct` is estimated from
a small sample and is the single most commonly wrong statistic in
PostgreSQL — which is why `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET (n_distinct =
...)` exists.

**Percentiles from a sample converge fast in the middle and slowly in the
tail.** A 5% sample gives a good median and a poor p99, because the tail is
where the rows are scarce. If the decision depends on p99, sample more, or
keep an exact histogram.

**Rollups make the rest unnecessary.** A daily aggregate of a million-row
table is a few thousand rows, is exact, and answers most questions instantly.
Sampling is what you do when you cannot pre-aggregate, not the first tool
you reach for.

## ex1 — a reproducible sample

What this tested: the syntax and the scaling. The estimate is
`avg × population`, or equivalently `sample_sum / sampling_fraction`, and the
second form is worth knowing because it generalises to stratified designs.
The classic mistake is omitting `REPEATABLE` and being unable to reproduce
last week's figure.

## ex2 — rows versus pages

What this tested: that the two methods are not interchangeable. Their row
counts differ — `SYSTEM` returns whole pages so the count is granular — and
their averages differ by more than sampling noise whenever physical order
correlates with the measure. The classic mistake is choosing `SYSTEM` for
speed without checking whether the table is clustered on anything that
matters.

## ex3 — hash sampling

What this tested: turning a key into a uniform pseudo-random number. `md5`
gives 128 bits; taking eight hex characters and casting through `bit(32)` to
`int` gives a well-distributed signed integer, and `% 100 = 0` selects about
one percent. The classic mistake is `id % 100 = 0`, which is deterministic
and *not* random — it correlates with anything else that correlates with the
id, such as signup order.

## ex4 — stratified

What this tested: that a uniform hash preserves strata automatically. Each
country's sample rate should be near 1%, with the small countries varying
most — which is the whole argument for stratified sampling when a rare
subgroup matters: sample it at a higher rate and weight it back.

## ex5 — the free row count

What this tested: `pg_class.reltuples`, and the discipline of quoting an
error. It is a `real`, so cast it; it is -1 on a table that has never been
analysed, which is a case worth handling rather than dividing by.

## ex6 — the free distinct count

What this tested: the sign convention. Negative `n_distinct` is a ratio and
must be multiplied by the row count. The classic mistake is reporting -0.1 as
a distinct count.

## ex7 — a percentile from a sample

What this tested: how much accuracy 5% buys in the middle of a distribution.
`total` is roughly uniform in this dataset, so the sample median lands very
close. Repeat the same comparison at p99 and the story changes; that
asymmetry is the point.

## ex8 — the rollup

What this tested: the alternative to all of the above. The compression ratio
is the headline and the equality check is the proof: a rollup that does not
reproduce the source total exactly has a bug, and checking it is the
reconciliation habit from the previous sector applied to your own
infrastructure.

## challenge — an estimate with an error bar

What this tested: that an estimate without an interval is a number pretending
to be a fact. The standard error of a sampled total is
`N × s / sqrt(n)`, optionally shrunk by the finite population correction
`sqrt(1 - n/N)`. At 1% that correction is negligible; at 50% it is not.

## review1 — cluster sampling

Sampling customers rather than orders changes what the sample is *of*. Per
customer statistics are only computable this way, and the price is higher
variance: you draw fewer independent units, and customers vary in how many
orders they have. Every sampling design trades those two against each other.

## Further reading

- [`SELECT` — `TABLESAMPLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the clause, the two built-in methods, and `REPEATABLE`.
- [`tsm_system_rows`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tsm-system-rows.html) — sampling a fixed number of rows rather than a percentage.
- [Statistics Used by the Planner](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/planner-stats.html) — `reltuples`, `n_distinct`, histograms, and how `ANALYZE` produces them.
- [`pg_class`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/catalog-pg-class.html) and [`pg_stats`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/view-pg-stats.html) — the catalog columns these exercises read.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — `stddev_samp`, `percentile_cont`, `percentile_disc`.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·F8 — Sampling, approximate aggregates and reporting at scale

The archive version: why exact is expensive, what the alternatives cost, and
how to quote an error.

## 1. Why exact aggregates are expensive

- **`count(*)`** — every row's visibility depends on the reading
  transaction's snapshot, so there is no maintained counter. An index-only
  scan over a small index can beat a heap scan when the visibility map is
  current, but it is still a scan.
- **`count(DISTINCT x)`** — sorts or hashes the whole column, per group,
  and does not share a pass with other aggregates.
- **`percentile_cont`** — an ordered-set aggregate: it materialises and
  sorts the input.
- **`ORDER BY random() LIMIT n`** — sorts the entire table. Never do this.

## 2. `TABLESAMPLE`

```sql
FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (42)
FROM orders TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM    (1) REPEATABLE (42)
```

|  | `BERNOULLI` | `SYSTEM` |
|---|---|---|
| unit | row | page |
| I/O | full scan | proportional to *p* |
| bias | none | clustering |
| row count | ≈ p% of rows | granular, in page-sized lumps |

`SYSTEM` is the fast one and the dangerous one. It takes every row in the
pages it selects, so any correlation between physical order and your measure
becomes bias. Tables written in time order — clickstreams, logs, append-only
event tables — are exactly the case where that correlation is total.

Two contrib methods extend the list:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION tsm_system_rows;
SELECT * FROM orders TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM_ROWS (1000);   -- exactly 1000 rows
CREATE EXTENSION tsm_system_time;
SELECT * FROM orders TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM_TIME (250);    -- as many as fit in 250 ms
```

`SYSTEM_ROWS` is the one to reach for when you want a fixed-size sample
rather than a fixed fraction.

## 3. Hash sampling

```sql
-- ~1% of customers, deterministic, stable across tables and runs
WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0
```

Why not `id % 100 = 0`? Because ids are not random. They correlate with
signup order, with migration batches, with whatever the sequence did during
an incident. A hash destroys that structure; a modulus preserves it.

The property that matters: **the same key hashes the same way everywhere**.
A 1% hash sample of `customers` joined to a 1% hash sample of `orders` on
`customer_id` gives you all the orders of the sampled customers. Two
independent `TABLESAMPLE` calls give you almost nothing, because the
intersection of two independent 1% samples is 0.01%.

## 4. Sampling designs

- **Simple random** — `BERNOULLI`, or a hash on the primary key. Unbiased,
  easy, and useless for rare subgroups.
- **Stratified** — sample each subgroup at its own rate and weight back.
  Necessary when a small stratum matters: 1% of a country with 200 customers
  is two customers.
- **Cluster** — sample entities and take all their rows (the hash-on-key
  design). Required for per-entity statistics; higher variance, because
  entities differ in size.

Scaling up a sample:

```sql
sum(x) / (sample_n::numeric / population_n)      -- ratio estimator
avg(x) * population_n                            -- equivalent for a total
```

Use the achieved sample size, not the requested percentage. `BERNOULLI (1)`
does not return exactly 1%.

## 5. Catalog estimates

```sql
SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'orders'::regclass;

SELECT n_distinct FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'customer_id';
```

`n_distinct` semantics:

- **positive** — an absolute estimate of the number of distinct values.
- **negative** — a ratio to the row count. `-0.5` means "half the rows are
  distinct". This is how the planner expresses cardinality that scales with
  the table.
- Convert: `CASE WHEN n_distinct < 0 THEN -n_distinct * reltuples ELSE
  n_distinct END`.

`reltuples` is `-1` on a relation that has never been analysed. Both values
are as fresh as the last `ANALYZE`; check `pg_stat_user_tables.last_analyze`
before quoting them.

Free row-count estimate for an arbitrary query — read the planner's guess:

```sql
EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid';
```

The top node's `Plan Rows` is an estimate that costs no scan at all. It is
often within a factor of two and occasionally out by a thousand; use it for
"is this big or small", never for a reported figure.

## 6. Approximate distincts

PostgreSQL has no built-in HyperLogLog. The options, in order of preference:

1. **`postgres-hll` extension.** Fixed-size sketches (about 1.2 KB for ~2%
   error), mergeable — you can union two days' sketches and get the distinct
   count of both, which is the property that makes rollups of distinct counts
   possible at all.
2. **`pg_stats.n_distinct`.** Free, whole-column only, frequently wrong.
3. **Sample and extrapolate.** Tempting and mathematically bad: distinct
   counts do not scale linearly with sampling rate, because rare values are
   likely to be missed entirely. A 1% sample of a column with a million
   distinct values does not have ten thousand of them in any predictable way.

Point 3 is worth dwelling on. Sums and means extrapolate; **distinct counts
do not**. That asymmetry is the reason sketches exist.

## 7. Rollups

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_category_revenue AS
SELECT date_trunc('day', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
       p.category,
       count(*) AS lines,
       sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue
FROM order_items i
JOIN orders o   ON o.id = i.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

A million line items become a few thousand rows: exact, instant, and enough
for almost every question anyone asks. Sampling is what you do when you
cannot pre-aggregate — a new dimension, an ad-hoc question, a cardinality
that does not roll up.

What does not roll up: distinct counts (unless you store sketches), medians
and percentiles (unless you store t-digests or full histograms), and anything
that needs row-level detail. Sums, counts, minima and maxima roll up
perfectly, which is why every warehouse fact table is made of them.

## 8. Common mistakes

- `ORDER BY random() LIMIT 10` on a large table.
- `TABLESAMPLE` without `REPEATABLE` in anything reproducible.
- `SYSTEM` on a table clustered on something correlated with the measure.
- Joining two independent samples.
- `id % 100 = 0` as a "random" sample.
- Extrapolating a distinct count from a sample.
- Reporting `n_distinct` without handling the negative convention.
- Quoting `reltuples` without checking when it was last analysed.
- Scaling by the requested percentage rather than the achieved sample size.
- An estimate with no interval.
- Sampling when a rollup would have been exact and faster.

## 9. The interview answer

> *"The dashboard's count query takes 40 seconds. What do you do?"*

"First I ask what precision the number needs, because `count(*)` is a scan —
MVCC means visibility is per-transaction, so there's no counter to read. If
'about right' is fine, `pg_class.reltuples` is free, and I'd quote it with
the last-analyze time. If it needs to be closer, a `TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI`
with a `REPEATABLE` seed and a scaled-up estimate with a confidence interval.
But the real answer is usually a rollup: pre-aggregate to a daily
materialized view and the number becomes exact and instant. Sampling is for
what you can't pre-aggregate. And the one thing that doesn't work is
extrapolating a distinct count from a sample — distincts don't scale
linearly, which is what HyperLogLog sketches exist for."

## Check yourself

1. Why is `count(*)` not O(1) in PostgreSQL?
2. Contrast `BERNOULLI` and `SYSTEM` on unit, I/O and bias.
3. Give a table where `SYSTEM` sampling is badly biased and say why.
4. What does `REPEATABLE` change, and when is omitting it defensible?
5. Why does joining two `TABLESAMPLE` results produce almost nothing?
6. Write a deterministic 1% hash sample and explain why `id % 100` is worse.
7. What does a negative `n_distinct` mean, and how do you convert it?
8. When is `reltuples` -1?
9. Why can't you extrapolate a distinct count from a sample?
10. Which aggregates roll up and which do not?
11. Give the standard error of a sampled total, and say what the finite
    population correction does.
12. You need a p99 from a sample. What changes compared with a median?
13. Name three ways to get a row-count estimate without scanning.
lessons.fullReading:
# The long read — the price of being exactly right

## Where `TABLESAMPLE` came from

`TABLESAMPLE` is SQL:2003 and PostgreSQL implemented it in 9.5 (2016), rather
late, and with an extensibility hook that is more interesting than the
feature itself. The two methods in the standard — `BERNOULLI` and `SYSTEM` —
are hard-coded in most implementations. PostgreSQL made the sampling method a
pluggable interface: a method is a function returning a
`tsm_handler`, with callbacks for "which block next" and "which tuple in this
block", so `tsm_system_rows` and `tsm_system_time` are ordinary extensions
rather than core changes. Anyone can write a sampler.

The naming is unhelpfully abstract. `BERNOULLI` means a Bernoulli trial per
row: flip a biased coin for every tuple. `SYSTEM` means "whatever the system
finds convenient", which in every implementation means block sampling. The
standard chose those names precisely so that `SYSTEM` could mean something
different on a different engine — which is a good argument for never assuming
its behaviour is portable.

The bias in `SYSTEM` deserves to be stated more strongly than the
documentation states it. It is not a small statistical wrinkle; it can be
total. Consider a table written in strict timestamp order, which describes
every clickstream, log table and append-only event store ever built. A 1%
`SYSTEM` sample selects roughly 1% of the *blocks*, so you get a handful of
contiguous time windows and every row inside them. Any question about
behaviour over time answered from that sample is answered from a few hours of
history. The rows are real; the sample is not random in the dimension you
care about.

## MVCC and the count

The perennial complaint that "PostgreSQL can't count" deserves its proper
explanation, because the reason is a design decision with compensating
benefits, not an oversight.

In PostgreSQL, a row version carries the transaction ids that created and
deleted it, and whether a given transaction can see it depends on that
transaction's snapshot. Two concurrent transactions can legitimately disagree
about how many rows a table has, and both are correct. There is therefore no
single number that could be cached. MySQL's MyISAM engine could return an
instant count because it had no MVCC; InnoDB, which does, cannot either.

What PostgreSQL offers instead:

- **Index-only scans.** When the visibility map says a page is all-visible,
  the executor need not consult the heap. A `count(*)` over a small index on
  an append-mostly, well-vacuumed table can be an order of magnitude cheaper
  than a heap scan — still a scan, but of much less data.
- **`reltuples`.** Maintained by `ANALYZE` and `VACUUM`, free to read.
- **Trigger-maintained counters.** A summary table updated by row triggers.
  Exact, and a serialisation point: every insert now contends on one row.
  Sometimes right, often a scalability disaster in disguise.

## Estimation error, honestly

For a simple random sample of size *n* from a population of *N*, the
estimated total is `N × x̄` and its standard error is

```
SE = N × s / sqrt(n) × sqrt(1 - n/N)
```

where *s* is the sample standard deviation. The last factor is the **finite
population correction**: it shrinks the error as the sample approaches a
census, and is negligible until the sampling fraction gets large. At 1% it
multiplies by 0.995 and can be ignored; at 50% it multiplies by 0.71 and
cannot.

The 95% interval is `estimate ± 1.96 × SE`, which relies on the sampling
distribution being approximately normal — reliable for sums and means at
sample sizes in the thousands, and unreliable for anything heavy-tailed. If a
handful of enormous orders dominate the revenue, a 1% sample either catches
one or does not, and the estimate is bimodal rather than normal. The
practical cure is stratification: take the big accounts as a census and
sample the long tail.

The deeper point is that the interval is part of the number. An estimate
quoted without one invites the reader to treat it as exact, and the first
time it moves by 3% they will investigate a business change that never
happened.

## Why distinct counts are different

Sums and means are **linear**: each sampled row contributes independently, so
scaling by the inverse sampling fraction is unbiased. Distinct counts are
not. Whether a value appears in your sample depends on how many rows carry
it, so rare values are systematically missed and common values are found
every time. A 1% sample of a column with a million distinct values, each
appearing once, contains about ten thousand distinct values — and there is no
way to recover the million from that number without assuming a distribution.

This is why probabilistic sketches exist. **HyperLogLog** hashes each value
and tracks the maximum number of leading zeros seen, which is a
distribution-free estimator of cardinality: it needs about 1.2 KB for a few
percent error at any cardinality, and — crucially — two sketches can be
merged by taking element-wise maxima. That mergeability is what makes
distinct counts roll up: store a sketch per day, union them for a month, and
get the monthly distinct count without re-reading the raw data. PostgreSQL
does not ship it; the `postgres-hll` extension does, and any warehouse doing
serious unique-user reporting has an equivalent.

The same logic applies to percentiles. Means and sums roll up; medians do
not, because the median of daily medians is not the monthly median.
**t-digest** and similar sketches are the answer, and they are mergeable for
the same reason.

## Performance notes

- **`BERNOULLI` saves CPU, not I/O.** If the query is I/O bound, it will not
  help. `SYSTEM` saves both, at the cost of the bias.
- **Hash sampling is a filter, not a scan reduction.** `md5(id::text)` is
  evaluated per row, so a hash sample reads the whole table and computes a
  hash for each row — slower per row than no filter at all. Its value is
  determinism and join stability, not speed. If speed matters, materialise
  the sampled key set once.
- **An expression index can make it fast.** Indexing the hash expression
  turns the sample into an index scan, which is worth doing if the same
  sample is queried repeatedly.
- **`ANALYZE` cost is proportional to the statistics target**, not to the
  table: it reads a bounded sample of pages. Raising
  `default_statistics_target` for a skewed column is cheap and often fixes an
  `n_distinct` that is wrecking your plans.
- **Rollups want incremental maintenance.** `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`
  recomputes everything; a rollup table updated by an hourly job that only
  reads new rows scales with the increment rather than the history.

## When not to approximate

- **Money, invoices, regulatory reporting, anything auditable.** Nobody wants
  an estimated tax return. Exactness is a requirement, and the answer to slow
  is a rollup or an index, not a sample.
- **Small tables.** Sampling a hundred thousand rows to avoid a scan is
  optimising the wrong thing and adds a source of error for no benefit.
- **When the subgroup you care about is rare.** A 1% sample of a country with
  two hundred customers has two of them. Either stratify or do not sample.
- **When the number is a threshold trigger.** "Alert if fewer than 100 rows
  arrived" cannot be answered by an estimate that is ±10%.
- **When you cannot explain the error to the reader.** An approximation you
  cannot put an interval on is not an approximation; it is a guess with a
  decimal point, and it will be quoted back to you as a fact.

## The habit worth building

Before optimising an aggregate, ask what decision the number feeds and what
precision that decision needs. Most dashboard numbers are looked at to see
whether something is roughly where it was yesterday, and for that a
`reltuples` estimate quoted with its staleness is better than an exact number
that costs forty seconds and is stale by the time it renders. The small
number of figures that genuinely need to be exact deserve a rollup, an index,
and a reconciliation check — not a faster scan.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — a reproducible sample

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Take a **1% Bernoulli sample** of `orders` with
seed **42**, and scale the result back up to an estimate of total revenue.

Columns, in this order:

1. `sampled_orders` — how many rows the sample actually returned
2. `avg_total` — the mean `total` in the sample, rounded to 2 decimals
3. `est_total_revenue` — the estimated revenue of the whole table, rounded
   to 2 decimals

One row.

Estimate with `avg_total × (SELECT count(*) FROM orders)`. Note that the
population count is exact and cheap enough here; in a real approximation you
would use `reltuples` for that too, which ex5 covers.

`REPEATABLE (42)` is what makes the answer the same every time you run it.
Without it the sample — and therefore the estimate — changes on every
execution, which makes the report irreproducible and this exercise
ungradeable.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`TABLESAMPLE` goes in the `FROM` clause, immediately after the table name. It
samples the table, before any `WHERE` or aggregation.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS sampled_orders,
       round(avg(total), 2) AS avg_total,
       round(avg(total) * (SELECT count(*) FROM orders), 2) AS est_total_revenue
FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (42);
```

## Hint 3

`BERNOULLI (1)` flips an independent coin per row, so it returns
approximately — not exactly — one percent. That is why the estimate uses
`avg × N` rather than `sum × 100`: the mean is unbiased regardless of how many
rows the coin happened to select, while multiplying the sum by a fixed 100
assumes a sample size you did not get. Decide which form you would use for a
count rather than a total.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run it twice with the seed, then twice without, and watch the numbers. The
seeded version is identical every time; the unseeded one moves by a fraction
of a percent on each execution. Now imagine explaining to a stakeholder why
last Tuesday's figure and today's figure differ when nothing happened. That
conversation is what `REPEATABLE` prevents.

## Hint 2

Compare your estimate with the truth: `SELECT sum(total) FROM orders`. It
should be close, and "close" is doing a lot of work in that sentence — the
challenge exercise makes it precise with a confidence interval. An estimate
whose error you cannot quantify is a number pretending to be a fact.

## Hint 3

Note what `BERNOULLI` did and did not save. It read every page of the table —
the coin flip is per row, so the rows must be read to be flipped — and saved
you the cost of aggregating 99% of them. On an I/O-bound query that is no
saving at all, which is the entire argument for `SYSTEM` and the entire
reason ex2 exists.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex1 — a seeded Bernoulli sample, scaled back up.
SELECT count(*)                                                    AS sampled_orders,
       round(avg(total), 2)                                        AS avg_total,
       round(avg(total) * (SELECT count(*) FROM orders), 2)        AS est_total_revenue
FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (42);
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex1 — same sample, estimate built in an outer level.
WITH s AS (
    SELECT total
    FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (42)
), pop AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS n FROM orders
)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM s)                                    AS sampled_orders,
       round((SELECT sum(total) FROM s) / (SELECT count(*) FROM s), 2) AS avg_total,
       round((SELECT sum(total) FROM s) / (SELECT count(*) FROM s)
             * (SELECT n FROM pop), 2)                             AS est_total_revenue
FROM pop;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — rows versus pages

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The two sampling methods, at the same rate and the
same seed, side by side.

Columns, in this order:

1. `method` — the text `'bernoulli'` or `'system'`
2. `rows` — how many rows that method returned
3. `avg_total` — the mean `total` in that sample, 2 decimals

**Ordered by `method` ascending.** Two rows. Both at 1%, both
`REPEATABLE (42)`.

`BERNOULLI` flips a coin per row. `SYSTEM` picks *pages* and takes every row
in them — far less I/O, and clustered, so any correlation between physical
row order and your measure becomes bias. Notice how much less granular the
`SYSTEM` row count is: it comes in page-sized lumps, because that is the unit
it samples.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two independent one-row queries, `UNION ALL`ed, each labelling itself. The
only difference between them is the method keyword.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT 'bernoulli' AS method, count(*) AS rows, round(avg(total), 2) AS avg_total
FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (42)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'system', count(*), round(avg(total), 2)
FROM orders TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1) REPEATABLE (42)
ORDER BY method;
```

## Hint 3

The same seed does **not** give you the same rows from the two methods — the
seed feeds a different selection process in each, one over rows and one over
blocks. It only guarantees that each method returns the same sample every
time *it* runs. Decide what you would compare if you wanted to measure the
bias rather than observe it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about where the bias would come from on each table in this dataset.
`orders.total` was generated independently of insertion order, so a block
sample of `orders` is reasonably well behaved. `events.ts` is strictly
increasing with `id`, so the table is physically ordered by time — and a 1%
`SYSTEM` sample of `events` is a sample of a few contiguous time windows, not
a sample of the month. Any question about behaviour over time answered from
that sample is answered from a few hours of history.

## Hint 2

That difference is not a statistical nicety, it is a total failure in the
dimension you care about. And the output looks perfect: real rows, plausible
values, a tidy average. The only way to catch it is to know how the table is
physically ordered before choosing the method — which is a fact about the
storage, not about the data.

## Hint 3

Weigh the trade honestly. `SYSTEM` at 1% reads roughly 1% of the pages, so on
a large table it is a hundred times cheaper. `BERNOULLI` reads everything.
When the table has no meaningful physical ordering — a hash-distributed
table, or one that has been through enough updates to be thoroughly shuffled
— `SYSTEM` is close to free and close to unbiased, and that combination is
why it exists.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex2 — row sampling and page sampling, compared.
SELECT 'bernoulli' AS method,
       count(*) AS rows,
       round(avg(total), 2) AS avg_total
FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (42)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'system',
       count(*),
       round(avg(total), 2)
FROM orders TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1) REPEATABLE (42)
ORDER BY method;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex2 — same two samples, aggregated in CTEs first.
WITH b AS (
    SELECT total FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (42)
), s AS (
    SELECT total FROM orders TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1) REPEATABLE (42)
), summary AS (
    SELECT 'bernoulli'::text AS method,
           (SELECT count(*) FROM b) AS rows,
           (SELECT round(sum(total) / count(*), 2) FROM b) AS avg_total
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'system',
           (SELECT count(*) FROM s),
           (SELECT round(sum(total) / count(*), 2) FROM s)
)
SELECT method, rows, avg_total
FROM summary
ORDER BY method;

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — hash sampling

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. `TABLESAMPLE` picks different rows in every table,
so a 1% sample of `customers` and a 1% sample of `orders` share almost
nothing. Hashing a key instead picks the same **entities** everywhere, and
gives the same answer on every run without a seed.

Take approximately 1% of `customers` by hashing `id`:

```sql
('x' || substr(md5(id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0
```

Columns, in this order:

1. `sampled_customers` — how many customers the hash selected
2. `est_total_customers` — `sampled_customers * 100`
3. `actual_customers` — `count(*)` over the whole table

One row.

Read the expression: `md5` gives 32 hex characters, `substr(..., 1, 8)` takes
eight of them, `'x' || …` makes a hex literal PostgreSQL can cast to
`bit(32)`, and that casts to a signed `int`. The modulus selects roughly one
value in a hundred. Note that `% 100 = 0` matches negative multiples too,
which is what keeps the rate near 1% rather than near 0.5%.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An ordinary `WHERE` clause. There is no sampling machinery involved — the
hash turns the key into a well-distributed number and you keep one bucket of
it.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT count(*) FILTER (
           WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0
       ) AS sampled_customers,
       ...
FROM customers;
```

Computing both the sample and the population in one pass avoids reading the
table twice.

## Hint 3

Do not be tempted by `id % 100 = 0`. It is deterministic, it is one
character shorter, and it is not random: ids correlate with signup order,
with migration batches, with whatever the sequence did during an incident.
Every one of those correlations survives the modulus and contaminates your
sample. The hash destroys the structure; the modulus preserves it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The property to internalise is **join stability**. Apply the same expression
to `orders.customer_id` and you get exactly the orders of exactly these
customers — the same slice of the world in every table, computed
independently, with no coordination and no seed. Two `TABLESAMPLE` calls
cannot do that: the intersection of two independent 1% samples is 0.01%.

## Hint 2

Second property: **stability over time**. A customer sampled today is sampled
next month, because the hash depends only on the id. That makes hash sampling
the right tool for a longitudinal study, a canary cohort, or a feature
rollout — the same 1% of users, every day, without storing a list.

## Hint 3

Understand what it costs. The hash is evaluated per row, so this reads the
whole table and does an `md5` for every row — slower per row than no filter
at all. Its value is determinism and join stability, not speed. If the same
sample is queried repeatedly, index the expression, or materialise the
sampled key set once and join to it.

references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex3 — sample and population computed separately.
WITH sampled AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM customers
    WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0
)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM sampled)       AS sampled_customers,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM sampled) * 100 AS est_total_customers,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM customers)     AS actual_customers;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — stratified

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Check that the hash sample is uniform across
subgroups: a good sampler should hit roughly the same rate in every country.

Columns, in this order:

1. `country`
2. `customers` — all customers in that country
3. `sampled` — how many of them the 1% hash selected
4. `pct_sampled` — `sampled` as a percentage of `customers`, 2 decimals

**Ordered by `country` ascending.** Twelve rows. Same hash expression as ex3.

The rates should all be near 1, with the smallest countries varying most —
which is the entire argument for stratified sampling. One percent of a
country with 200 customers is two customers, and no conclusion should be
drawn from two customers. The fix is to sample small strata at a higher rate
and weight them back.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One grouped pass over `customers`: the total is `count(*)`, the sample is a
filtered count with the hash predicate, the rate is their ratio.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT country,
       count(*) AS customers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0)
           AS sampled,
       ...
FROM customers GROUP BY country ORDER BY country;
```

## Hint 3

`100.0` in the ratio, as always, or integer division truncates every rate to
0 or 1. Look at the spread of `pct_sampled` across the twelve rows and think
about what it would take to be confident about the smallest one — then decide
what sample size you would demand before publishing a per-country figure.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This exercise is really a test of the sampler, not of the data. A uniform
hash should produce rates scattered around 1% with variance inversely
proportional to the stratum size. If one country came back at 4% or 0%, the
hash is correlated with country — which would happen if you used `id % 100`
and ids had been assigned in country batches. Checking the sampler against
the strata is a habit worth having.

## Hint 2

Now think about the design this motivates. If a question is about the
smallest country, simple random sampling is the wrong tool no matter how
uniform it is: 1% of 200 is 2. A stratified design takes, say, 1% of the
large countries and 20% of the small ones, then weights each stratum by the
inverse of its own rate when scaling back up. The arithmetic is easy; knowing
that you need it is the skill.

## Hint 3

Consider the third design too. Sampling *customers* is cluster sampling as
soon as you follow them into `orders` — you draw whole entities, not rows,
and entities differ in size. That raises the variance of any per-order
statistic computed from the sample, because a single sampled customer with
forty orders swings it. Every sampling design trades bias, variance and cost;
naming which one you chose is part of reporting the number.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex4 — is the hash uniform across strata?
SELECT country,
       count(*) AS customers,
       count(*) FILTER (
           WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0
       ) AS sampled,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (
           WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0
       ) / count(*), 2) AS pct_sampled
FROM customers
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY country;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex4 — flag first, then aggregate the flag.
WITH flagged AS (
    SELECT country,
           (('x' || substr(md5(id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0) AS in_sample
    FROM customers
)
SELECT country,
       count(*) AS customers,
       sum(in_sample::int) AS sampled,
       round(100.0 * sum(in_sample::int) / count(*), 2) AS pct_sampled
FROM flagged
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY country;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — the free row count

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. `count(*)` on a large table is a scan, because MVCC
makes visibility per-transaction and there is no counter to read. The planner
keeps an estimate anyway, and reading it costs nothing.

Compare the two for `orders`.

Columns, in this order:

1. `exact_rows` — `count(*)`
2. `estimated_rows` — `pg_class.reltuples` for `orders`, as a `bigint`
3. `pct_error` — `100 * (estimated_rows - exact_rows) / exact_rows`, 4
   decimals

One row.

Find the catalog row with `WHERE oid = 'orders'::regclass` — that resolves
the name through the search path and cannot match a same-named table in
another schema. `reltuples` is a `real`, and it is `-1` on a relation that
has never been analysed, which is a case a production version should handle
rather than divide by.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two numbers from two places: one aggregate over the table, one lookup in the
system catalog. Neither depends on the other, so scalar subqueries are the
natural shape.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM orders) AS exact_rows,
       (SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'orders'::regclass)
           AS estimated_rows,
       ...
```

## Hint 3

Compute the percentage from the same two subqueries, or wrap them in a CTE
and do the arithmetic outside — the second reads better and evaluates each
once. `reltuples` is a `real` (four-byte float), so cast before comparing,
and remember that the estimate is exactly as fresh as the last `ANALYZE`.
Decide what you would report alongside the estimate to make it trustworthy.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Quote the staleness with the number. `pg_stat_user_tables` has
`last_analyze` and `last_autoanalyze` for every table; an estimate from
yesterday on an append-only table is excellent, and the same estimate on a
table that was bulk-loaded an hour ago is fiction. "Approximately 500,000, as
of the 04:00 analyze" is a usable statement; "approximately 500,000" is not.

## Hint 2

There is a third estimator worth knowing about, and it works for an arbitrary
query rather than a whole table:

```sql
EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid';
```

The top node's `Plan Rows` is the planner's guess, and it costs no scan at
all. It is usually within a factor of two and occasionally out by a thousand.
Use it for "is this big or small", never for a reported figure.

## Hint 3

Consider the exact-and-fast option people reach for and usually regret: a
counter table maintained by row triggers. It gives an exact count in constant
time, and it turns every insert into a contention point on one row, which
serialises your write path. On a busy table that is a much worse problem than
a slow count. Rollups and estimates exist because the obvious fix does not
scale.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex5 — the planner's row count, and its error.
WITH nums AS (
    SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM orders) AS exact_rows,
           (SELECT reltuples::bigint
            FROM pg_class
            WHERE oid = 'orders'::regclass) AS estimated_rows
)
SELECT exact_rows,
       estimated_rows,
       round(100.0 * (estimated_rows - exact_rows) / exact_rows, 4) AS pct_error
FROM nums;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex5 — same comparison, catalog read inline.
SELECT c.n AS exact_rows,
       p.reltuples::bigint AS estimated_rows,
       round(100.0 * (p.reltuples::bigint - c.n) / c.n, 4) AS pct_error
FROM (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM orders) c
CROSS JOIN pg_class p
WHERE p.oid = 'orders'::regclass;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the free distinct count

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. `count(DISTINCT x)` sorts or hashes the whole
column. `ANALYZE` already estimated it and put the answer in `pg_stats`.

Compare the two for `orders.customer_id`.

Columns, in this order:

1. `exact_distinct` — `count(DISTINCT customer_id)`
2. `estimated_distinct` — from `pg_stats.n_distinct`, converted to an
   absolute `bigint`
3. `pct_error` — `100 * (estimated_distinct - exact_distinct) /
   exact_distinct`, 2 decimals

One row.

The conversion is the exercise. `n_distinct` is **signed**: a positive value
is an absolute count of distinct values, and a **negative** value is a ratio
to the row count — `-0.5` means "half the rows are distinct", which is how
the planner expresses a cardinality that grows with the table. Convert with

```sql
CASE WHEN n_distinct < 0 THEN -n_distinct * reltuples ELSE n_distinct END
```

Reporting `-0.1` as a distinct count is the classic mistake, and it is not
subtle once you have seen it.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three ingredients: the exact count from `orders`, `n_distinct` from
`pg_stats`, and `reltuples` from `pg_class` for the conversion when
`n_distinct` is negative.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT n_distinct FROM pg_stats
WHERE schemaname = 'public' AND tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'customer_id';
```

`pg_stats` is a view over `pg_statistic` that resolves the column name for
you; without it you would be joining `pg_attribute` by attribute number.

## Hint 3

Round the converted estimate to a `bigint` before comparing, or the
percentage carries a fractional row. And note that `pg_stats` returns no row
at all for a column that has never been analysed — a production version
handles that with a `LEFT JOIN` or a `coalesce` rather than silently
returning nothing. Decide which failure you would rather have.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`n_distinct` is estimated from `ANALYZE`'s bounded sample and is the single
most commonly wrong statistic in PostgreSQL. Distinct counts are hard to
estimate from a sample for a fundamental reason — see the next hint — and
when it is wrong the planner picks bad join strategies. That is why
`ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET (n_distinct = -0.9)` exists: you can
overrule it when you know better than the sampler.

## Hint 2

Here is the fundamental reason, and it is the most important idea in this
sector. Sums and means are **linear**: each sampled row contributes
independently, so scaling by the inverse sampling fraction is unbiased.
Distinct counts are not. Whether a value appears in your sample depends on
how many rows carry it, so rare values are systematically missed and common
ones are always found. You cannot recover the true cardinality from a sample
without assuming a distribution.

## Hint 3

That asymmetry is why probabilistic sketches exist. HyperLogLog hashes each
value and tracks the longest run of leading zeros, which estimates
cardinality without any distributional assumption — a couple of kilobytes for
a few percent error at any scale. Crucially, two sketches merge by taking
element-wise maxima, so a distinct count *rolls up*: store one per day, union
them for a month. PostgreSQL does not ship it; the `postgres-hll` extension
does, and every warehouse doing unique-user reporting has an equivalent.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex6 — the planner's distinct estimate, sign convention and all.
WITH stat AS (
    SELECT s.n_distinct,
           (SELECT reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'orders'::regclass) AS reltuples
    FROM pg_stats s
    WHERE s.schemaname = 'public'
      AND s.tablename = 'orders'
      AND s.attname = 'customer_id'
), nums AS (
    SELECT (SELECT count(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders) AS exact_distinct,
           round(CASE WHEN stat.n_distinct < 0
                      THEN (-stat.n_distinct * stat.reltuples)::numeric
                      ELSE stat.n_distinct::numeric END)::bigint AS estimated_distinct
    FROM stat
)
SELECT exact_distinct,
       estimated_distinct,
       round(100.0 * (estimated_distinct - exact_distinct) / exact_distinct, 2) AS pct_error
FROM nums;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex6 — same numbers, conversion done with greatest/least logic.
SELECT e.exact_distinct,
       est.estimated_distinct,
       round(100.0 * (est.estimated_distinct - e.exact_distinct) / e.exact_distinct, 2)
           AS pct_error
FROM (SELECT count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS exact_distinct FROM orders) e
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT round(
               CASE WHEN s.n_distinct >= 0 THEN s.n_distinct::numeric
                    ELSE (-1)::numeric * s.n_distinct::numeric
                         * (SELECT reltuples FROM pg_class
                            WHERE oid = 'orders'::regclass)::numeric
               END)::bigint AS estimated_distinct
    FROM pg_stats s
    WHERE s.schemaname = 'public'
      AND s.tablename = 'orders'
      AND s.attname = 'customer_id'
) est;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a percentile from a sample

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. `percentile_cont` is an ordered-set aggregate: it
materialises and sorts its input. Find out how much of that work a 5% sample
saves you and what it costs in accuracy.

Columns, in this order:

1. `exact_median` — `percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total)`
   over all of `orders`, rounded to 2 decimals
2. `sample_median` — the same over a **5% Bernoulli sample, seed 7**, 2
   decimals
3. `abs_error` — `abs(sample_median - exact_median)`, 2 decimals
4. `pct_error` — `100 * abs_error / exact_median`, 3 decimals

One row.

`total` is roughly uniform between 5 and 2000 in this dataset, so the sample
median should land very close. Run the same comparison at `percentile_cont(0.99)`
afterwards and the story changes: the tail is where the rows are scarce, so a
sample estimates the middle well and the extremes badly. If your decision
depends on p99, sample more or keep a histogram.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two independent scalar values, then arithmetic. Compute each median in its
own CTE or scalar subquery so the two populations cannot get confused.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH exact AS (
    SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total) AS m FROM orders
), samp AS (
    SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total) AS m
    FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (5) REPEATABLE (7)
)
SELECT round(exact.m::numeric, 2), round(samp.m::numeric, 2), ...
FROM exact CROSS JOIN samp;
```

## Hint 3

`percentile_cont` returns `double precision` when given a `numeric` input, so
cast to `numeric` before `round(x, 2)` — `round(double precision, int)` is
not a function that exists. `percentile_disc` is the sibling that returns an
actual observed value rather than interpolating between two; decide which one
"the median order value" ought to mean.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the sample actually bought. The exact version sorts half a million
values; the sample sorts twenty-five thousand. That is a real saving and a
sub-second query either way at this size — the point is the ratio, which
holds when the table is a thousand times larger and the exact version stops
being viable.

## Hint 2

Now think about why medians do not roll up. The median of daily medians is
not the monthly median, and no amount of storage of daily medians will
recover it — unlike sums and counts, which combine perfectly. That is why
percentile sketches such as t-digest exist: they are mergeable summaries, so
you can store one per day and union them, exactly as HyperLogLog does for
distinct counts.

## Hint 3

Try `percentile_cont(0.99)` in place of `0.5` in both branches and compare
the errors. The median is estimated from the dense middle of the
distribution, where a 5% sample still has thousands of neighbouring
observations. The 99th percentile is estimated from the sparse tail, where it
has far fewer — so its error is larger and much more variable between seeds.
Any statement about "accuracy from a sample" that does not say which
statistic is a statement about nothing.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex7 — exact median versus a 5% sampled one.
WITH exact AS (
    SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total) AS m
    FROM orders
), samp AS (
    SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total) AS m
    FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (5) REPEATABLE (7)
)
SELECT round(exact.m::numeric, 2) AS exact_median,
       round(samp.m::numeric, 2)  AS sample_median,
       round(abs(samp.m - exact.m)::numeric, 2) AS abs_error,
       round((100 * abs(samp.m - exact.m) / exact.m)::numeric, 3) AS pct_error
FROM exact
CROSS JOIN samp;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex7 — the two medians gathered by a lateral join.
SELECT round(e.m::numeric, 2) AS exact_median,
       round(s.m::numeric, 2) AS sample_median,
       round((abs(s.m - e.m))::numeric, 2) AS abs_error,
       round((abs(s.m - e.m) * 100 / e.m)::numeric, 3) AS pct_error
FROM (SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total) AS m FROM orders) e
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total) AS m
    FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (5) REPEATABLE (7)
) s;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the rollup

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Before sampling anything, ask whether the question
could have been answered from a pre-aggregate. Usually it could.

Build a daily-by-category rollup of `order_items` (joined to `orders` for the
date and `products` for the category, all statuses), and report what it cost
and whether it is faithful.

Columns, in this order:

1. `source_rows` — `count(*)` over `order_items`
2. `rollup_rows` — how many rows the rollup has
3. `compression` — `source_rows / rollup_rows`, rounded to 1 decimal
4. `rollup_revenue` — `sum(revenue)` over the rollup, 2 decimals
5. `source_revenue` — `sum(quantity * price)` over `order_items`, 2 decimals
6. `verdict` — `'EXACT'` when the two revenues are equal, else `'DRIFT'`

One row.

The compression ratio is the headline; the equality check is the proof. A
rollup that does not reproduce the source total exactly has a bug, and
checking it is the previous sector's reconciliation habit applied to your own
infrastructure. Note that sums and counts roll up perfectly — and that
distinct counts and medians do not, which is the boundary of the technique.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Build the rollup in a CTE — one row per (day, category) — then compute all
six numbers from it and from the source.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH rollup AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('day', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
           p.category,
           count(*) AS lines,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN orders o   ON o.id = i.order_id
    JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
```

## Hint 3

`compression` divides two `bigint`s, so cast before dividing or you get a
truncated integer. For the verdict, both revenues are `numeric` sums of the
same `numeric` products, so exact equality is correct here and a tolerance
would be pretending to doubt something you have no reason to doubt. Decide
when that stops being true.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Look at the compression number and think about what it means for a dashboard.
A million line items become a few thousand rollup rows, which means every
question about daily revenue by category becomes instant, exact, and cheap
enough to run on every page load. Sampling is what you do when you cannot
pre-aggregate — a new dimension, an ad-hoc slice, a cardinality that will not
roll up. It is not the first tool to reach for.

## Hint 2

Now enumerate what does not roll up, because that boundary is the whole
design constraint of a warehouse. Sums, counts, minima and maxima combine
perfectly — which is exactly why every fact table is made of them. Averages
combine if you store the sum and the count separately, not if you store the
average. Distinct counts do not combine at all without a sketch. Medians and
percentiles do not combine without a t-digest.

## Hint 3

The production form of this is a materialized view refreshed nightly, or —
better — a rollup table that an hourly job appends to, reading only rows
newer than a watermark. `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` recomputes everything and
therefore gets slower forever; an incremental rollup scales with the
increment. Knowing that distinction before you build the first one saves a
migration later.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex8 — a daily rollup, its compression and its fidelity.
WITH rollup AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('day', o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
           p.category,
           count(*) AS lines,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN orders   o ON o.id = i.order_id
    JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY 1, 2
), src AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS source_rows,
           sum(quantity * price) AS source_revenue
    FROM order_items
)
SELECT src.source_rows,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM rollup) AS rollup_rows,
       round(src.source_rows::numeric / (SELECT count(*) FROM rollup), 1) AS compression,
       round((SELECT sum(revenue) FROM rollup), 2) AS rollup_revenue,
       round(src.source_revenue, 2) AS source_revenue,
       CASE WHEN (SELECT sum(revenue) FROM rollup) = src.source_revenue
            THEN 'EXACT' ELSE 'DRIFT' END AS verdict
FROM src;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / ex8 — the same figures assembled from separate aggregates.
WITH rollup AS (
    SELECT (o.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
           p.category,
           sum(i.quantity * i.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items i
    JOIN orders   o ON o.id = i.order_id
    JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY 1, 2
), r AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS rollup_rows, sum(revenue) AS rollup_revenue FROM rollup
), s AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS source_rows, sum(quantity * price) AS source_revenue
    FROM order_items
)
SELECT s.source_rows,
       r.rollup_rows,
       round(s.source_rows::numeric / r.rollup_rows, 1) AS compression,
       round(r.rollup_revenue, 2) AS rollup_revenue,
       round(s.source_revenue, 2) AS source_revenue,
       CASE WHEN r.rollup_revenue = s.source_revenue THEN 'EXACT' ELSE 'DRIFT' END AS verdict
FROM s CROSS JOIN r;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — an estimate with an error bar

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. An estimate without an interval is a number
pretending to be a fact. Estimate total order revenue from a 1% Bernoulli
sample at seed **99**, quote a 95% interval, and check whether the truth
falls inside it.

Columns, in this order:

1. `sample_n` — rows in the sample
2. `population_n` — `count(*)` over `orders`
3. `est_total` — `population_n * avg(total in sample)`, 2 decimals
4. `ci_low` — `est_total - 1.96 * SE`, 2 decimals
5. `ci_high` — `est_total + 1.96 * SE`, 2 decimals
6. `actual_total` — `sum(total)` over all of `orders`, 2 decimals
7. `within_ci` — boolean: is `actual_total` between `ci_low` and `ci_high`

One row. The standard error of a sampled total is

```
SE = population_n * stddev_samp(total) / sqrt(sample_n)
```

The finite population correction — multiplying by `sqrt(1 - n/N)` — is
negligible at a 1% sampling fraction and is omitted here; be able to say at
what fraction it stops being negligible.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Everything about the sample — count, mean, standard deviation — comes from
one pass over the sampled rows. The population size and true total come from
one pass over the table. Then it is arithmetic.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH s AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS n, avg(total) AS mean, stddev_samp(total) AS sd
    FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (99)
), p AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS n, sum(total) AS actual FROM orders
), est AS (
    SELECT s.n AS sample_n, p.n AS population_n,
           p.n * s.mean AS est_total,
           p.n * s.sd / sqrt(s.n) AS se,
           p.actual
    FROM s CROSS JOIN p
)
```

## Hint 3

`stddev_samp` divides by n-1 and is the right estimator for a sample;
`stddev_pop` divides by n and would understate the error slightly. `sqrt`
returns `double precision`, so the whole expression will need a `::numeric`
cast before `round(x, 2)`. Decide whether `within_ci` should use `BETWEEN`
and whether the endpoints should be inclusive.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand what the interval promises. It says that if you repeated this
sampling procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals produced would
contain the true total. It does **not** say there is a 95% probability that
this particular interval contains it — the true total is a fixed number and
this interval either contains it or does not. That distinction is pedantic in
conversation and important in a document somebody will act on.

## Hint 2

Interrogate the assumption behind the 1.96. It assumes the sampling
distribution of the mean is approximately normal, which holds for sums and
means at sample sizes in the thousands — the central limit theorem doing its
work. It fails when the distribution is heavy-tailed: if a handful of enormous
orders dominate the revenue, a 1% sample either catches one or does not, and
the estimate is bimodal rather than normal. `orders.total` here is roughly
uniform, so the assumption is safe; on real revenue data it very often is not,
and the cure is stratification — take the big accounts as a census and sample
the tail.

## Hint 3

Work out the finite population correction's magnitude yourself. At n/N = 0.01
the factor is `sqrt(0.99)` ≈ 0.995, which moves the interval by half a
percent of its own width — invisible. At n/N = 0.5 it is `sqrt(0.5)` ≈ 0.707,
which narrows the interval by nearly a third, and omitting it would make you
report an error bar that is 40% too wide. Knowing where a simplification stops
being safe is more useful than knowing the formula.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / challenge — a sampled total with a 95% interval.
WITH s AS (
    SELECT count(*)          AS n,
           avg(total)        AS mean,
           stddev_samp(total) AS sd
    FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (99)
), p AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS n, sum(total) AS actual FROM orders
), est AS (
    SELECT s.n AS sample_n,
           p.n AS population_n,
           (p.n * s.mean)::numeric              AS est_total,
           (p.n * s.sd / sqrt(s.n))::numeric    AS se,
           p.actual                             AS actual_total
    FROM s CROSS JOIN p
)
SELECT sample_n,
       population_n,
       round(est_total, 2)                       AS est_total,
       round(est_total - 1.96 * se, 2)           AS ci_low,
       round(est_total + 1.96 * se, 2)           AS ci_high,
       round(actual_total, 2)                    AS actual_total,
       (actual_total BETWEEN est_total - 1.96 * se
                         AND est_total + 1.96 * se) AS within_ci
FROM est;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / challenge — same interval, bounds computed in a CTE.
WITH s AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS n, avg(total) AS mean, stddev_samp(total) AS sd
    FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (99)
), p AS (
    SELECT count(*) AS n, sum(total) AS actual FROM orders
), bounds AS (
    SELECT s.n AS sample_n,
           p.n AS population_n,
           round((p.n * s.mean)::numeric, 2) AS est_total,
           round((p.n * s.mean - 1.96 * p.n * s.sd / sqrt(s.n))::numeric, 2) AS ci_low,
           round((p.n * s.mean + 1.96 * p.n * s.sd / sqrt(s.n))::numeric, 2) AS ci_high,
           round(p.actual, 2) AS actual_total
    FROM s CROSS JOIN p
)
SELECT sample_n, population_n, est_total, ci_low, ci_high, actual_total,
       (actual_total >= ci_low AND actual_total <= ci_high) AS within_ci
FROM bounds;

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — cluster sampling

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. Sampling *rows* and sampling *entities* are
different designs. Take approximately 1% of **customers** by hashing
`orders.customer_id`, which pulls in every order those customers placed.

Columns, in this order:

1. `sampled_customers` — distinct customers in the sample
2. `sampled_orders` — orders belonging to them
3. `avg_orders_per_customer` — `sampled_orders / sampled_customers`, 2
   decimals

One row. Use the same hash expression as ex3, applied to `customer_id`:

```sql
('x' || substr(md5(customer_id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0
```

This is the design that makes per-customer statistics computable from a
sample at all — a row sample would give you a fraction of each customer's
orders and no way to reconstruct their totals. The price is variance:
customers differ in how many orders they have, so a single unusual customer
moves any per-order statistic more than a row sample would.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3f08_sampling_approximation review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `WHERE` clause over `orders`, then two counts — one distinct, one not —
and a ratio.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS sampled_customers,
       count(*) AS sampled_orders,
       round(count(*)::numeric / count(DISTINCT customer_id), 2)
           AS avg_orders_per_customer
FROM orders
WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(customer_id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0;
```

## Hint 3

`count(*)::numeric` before the division, or you get integer truncation. Note
that `sampled_customers` here counts customers **who have orders** — the ones
with none never appear in this table at all, which is a population difference
worth being deliberate about. Decide whether that is the denominator you
want for "average orders per customer".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Compare against the truth: `SELECT count(*)::numeric / count(DISTINCT
customer_id) FROM orders`. Your sampled figure should be close, because a
uniform hash on the customer key selects customers independently of how many
orders they have. If it were systematically higher, the sampler would be
correlated with activity — which is exactly what happens if you sample
`orders` rows instead and then count distinct customers, because busy
customers are more likely to be caught.

## Hint 2

That last point is the trap this exercise exists to expose. Row sampling
`orders` and counting distinct customers gives a biased customer sample:
someone with forty orders is forty times more likely to appear than someone
with one. Any per-customer statistic computed from it is wrong in a direction
that flatters engagement. Sampling the *key* fixes it because the hash does
not know how many rows the key has.

## Hint 3

Now consider extending it. The same hash on `customer_id` applied to
`events`, `orders` and `customers` simultaneously gives a consistent 1% slice
of the whole world, joinable across all three, computed independently in each
query with no seed and no coordination. That is the property that makes hash
sampling the standard technique for building a shrunk development dataset —
and it is worth remembering the next time somebody proposes copying
production and deleting rows at random.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / review1 — sample entities, keep all their rows.
SELECT count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS sampled_customers,
       count(*)                    AS sampled_orders,
       round(count(*)::numeric / count(DISTINCT customer_id), 2)
           AS avg_orders_per_customer
FROM orders
WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(customer_id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3f08_sampling_approximation / review1 — customers reduced first, then their orders counted.
WITH sampled AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders
    FROM orders
    WHERE ('x' || substr(md5(customer_id::text), 1, 8))::bit(32)::int % 100 = 0
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT count(*)        AS sampled_customers,
       sum(orders)     AS sampled_orders,
       round(sum(orders)::numeric / count(*), 2) AS avg_orders_per_customer
FROM sampled;
